title: PATCH /api/v1/admin/users/{id} changes role but not the stored `scopes`, so a demoted admin keeps write/delete everywhere
reasoning:
I tried to refute this five ways and each attempt failed.

1. "A guard exists elsewhere in the call path." It does not. `require_write_auth` (core/security.py:569-588) is the only gate on the inventory write surface — 238 `Depends(require_write_auth)` sites across apps/backend/src/app/api/. It does not consult `request.state.token_scopes` at all; for a session user it loads the DB row and evaluates `role not in {"admin","editor"} and not has_scope(effective_scopes(user), "write", "*")`. `effective_scopes` (core/rbac.py:92-99) returns `defaults | explicit` whenever `explicit` is non-empty, so a stale explicit set can only ever widen, never narrow. There is no role check in any middleware (csrf, legacy_token, logging, rate_limit, security_headers, tenant) and no global write policy.

2. "The scenario is mistaken." Verified by running the real code:
   role: viewer / stored: ["admin:*","delete:*","read:*","write:*"] / effective: same four / require_write_auth 403? False / has_scope(admin,*)? True.

3. "The path is dead / needs an odd config." It is the product's only role-edit path. apps/frontend/src/api/client.jsx:403 `updateUser: (id, data) => client.patch('/admin/users/${id}', data)`, called from AdminUsersPage.jsx:309 with `{role, display_name}` — the admin UI's Edit User modal. Default configuration, no flags.

4. "The stale scopes are never actually written." They are, on every non-invite creation path: admin_users.py:195 (`POST /admin/users`), :267 (`POST /admin/users/local`), auth_service.py:507 (first-user register), :685 and :842 (bootstrap/OOBE) all persist `_scopes_for_role(role)` as an explicit JSON column (`User.scopes`, models.py:1960, `nullable=False, default="[]"`).

5. "Existing tests cover it." They cannot. `tests/factories.py:17-37` never sets `scopes`, so every factory user has `"[]"` and the union collapses to role defaults; `tests/test_users.py` asserts only the returned `role`/`is_active`. No test in the tree mentions demotion or asserts scopes after a role change.

Two corrections to the report, neither of which weakens it. (a) The routes are mounted under `/api/v1/admin/...`, not `/api/v1/users`. (b) The claim that nothing else rewrites `User.scopes` is wrong — `cli_admin.set_user_role` (scripts/cli_admin.py:637-640) does exactly `user.role = role; user.is_admin = ...; user.is_superuser = ...; user.scopes = _scopes_for_role(role)`. That strengthens the finding: the CLI establishes the intended convention and the HTTP endpoint is the one place that omits the last line.

Impact, on my own read rather than the report's. `is_superuser` *is* cleared at :335, so `require_role` still blocks the admin API surface by rank — the admin routes are not exposed. The real damage is the write/delete surface: an admin demoted to `viewer` retains `write:*` and `delete:*` and passes every `require_write_auth` route (hardware, networks, clusters, monitors, maps, docs, topologies, assets, misc) plus `require_scope("write","telemetry")` (api/telemetry.py:62). admin→editor demotion additionally leaves `delete:*` and `admin:*` behind. editor→viewer is safe by luck, because the editor defaults are per-resource (`write:hardware`, …) and `has_scope(scopes,"write","*")` does not match those. So this is an offboarding/least-privilege failure that silently does not take effect, with a UI that reports success and shows a read-only badge. High, not critical: it requires the account to have previously held admin, and it does not grant the admin API surface.

Not prevented by anything upstream: the payload role is validated against the three-role allowlist at :331 and the `require_role("admin")` gate protects the endpoint — both work fine. The defect is a missing write, not a missing check.
fix:
One line in `update_user`, matching `cli_admin.set_user_role` exactly. `_scopes_for_role` is already imported at admin_users.py:19, so no new import:

    if payload.role is not None:
        if payload.role not in ("admin", "editor", "viewer"):
            raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Invalid role")
        target.role = payload.role
        target.is_admin = payload.role == "admin"
        target.is_superuser = payload.role == "admin"
        target.scopes = _scopes_for_role(payload.role)   # <-- add

Re-deriving unconditionally (rather than only on downgrade) also repairs upgrades and keeps the column a pure function of the role, which is what every creation path already assumes.

Regression test, in apps/backend/tests/test_users.py alongside the existing PATCH cases — note it must construct the target with explicit scopes, since `factories.user` leaves them `"[]"` and that is precisely why the suite misses this today:

    async def test_demoted_admin_loses_write_scopes(client, auth_headers, factories):
        from app.services.auth_service import _scopes_for_role
        target = factories.user(role="admin", scopes=_scopes_for_role("admin"))
        resp = await client.patch(f"/api/v1/admin/users/{target.id}",
                                  headers=auth_headers, json={"role": "viewer"})
        assert resp.status_code == 200
        from app.core.rbac import effective_scopes, has_scope
        assert not has_scope(effective_scopes(target), "write", "*")

Separately, a one-shot data repair is warranted for anyone already demoted before the fix, since those rows stay over-privileged forever: `UPDATE users SET scopes = '["read:*"]' WHERE role IN ('viewer','demo') AND scopes LIKE '%write:%';` (and the editor equivalent). This is worth an Alembic migration rather than leaving it to operators, because there is no way for an admin to see or correct the stale column from the UI.

title: GitHub OAuth callback accepts an unverified email as the account key
reasoning:
Confirmed reachable end to end, and no guard exists anywhere else in the call path.

Reachability: line 637 reads `email = gh_user.get("email")`, the *public profile* email, which is null for any GitHub account that has not opted into publishing one — the default. So the `/user/emails` branch at 641-652 is the ordinary path, not an edge case. Inside it, `next((e["email"] for e in emails if e.get("primary") and e.get("verified")), None)` returns None whenever the account has no entry that is both primary and verified, and line 651-652 then takes `emails[0]["email"]` with no `verified` check at all.

Attacker control: the list is fetched with the attacker's own token from their own account. Adding an address is a normal account operation and the address is `verified: false` until the real owner clicks GitHub's confirmation link. An attacker who adds ops@corp.com and makes it their primary (verification still pending) has an email list with no primary+verified entry, so the fallback fires and returns the pending address, which GitHub returns first as the primary.

Impact: the string flows unchanged into `_upsert_oauth_user` (:375-420), which resolves the account with `db.query(User).filter(User.email == email).first()`. On a hit it logs into that existing row — it overwrites `user.provider` and stores tokens, but never compares a provider subject id, so there is no binding that could contradict the email. `_issue_jwt_and_redirect` then mints a full session for that row, whatever its role. `consume_invite_for_oauth` (user_service.py:333) likewise matches invites on email alone, so the same unverified string can also claim an invited role on a fresh account.

The auditor's scenario is slightly overstated in one respect: merely adding ops@corp.com while keeping a verified primary is not exploitable, because `next(...)` still finds the attacker's own primary. Exploitation requires the attacker's account to have no primary+verified entry — which is a state they can put their own account into, so it does not refute the finding.

Not covered by tests: grep for `github_callback` or `oauth/github/callback` across apps/backend/tests returns nothing. The only GitHub references in test_sec10_auth_controls.py exercise `_pop_state_or_400` (state single-use and expiry), not email selection. `git log -L 640,660` shows the fallback unchanged since the file was introduced, so it is legacy code no one revisited, not a considered decision.

Severity raised from the reported `low`: the outcome is pre-authentication takeover of an arbitrary existing account, admin rows included, needing only that the deployment enabled the shipped GitHub provider and that the attacker knows the target's email address. Note the same file's Google and OIDC callbacks also ignore `email_verified`, but that is a separate finding.
fix:
Delete the unverified fallback so the existing 400 handles the case. In `github_callback`, replace lines 651-652:

            if not email and emails:
                email = emails[0]["email"]

with nothing — control then falls through to the `if not email: raise HTTPException(400, "Could not obtain email from GitHub account")` at :655-656, which is already the right response.

If a fallback is genuinely wanted for accounts whose primary flag is absent, it must still require verification, matching the style of the existing `next(...)`:

            if not email:
                email = next((e["email"] for e in emails if e.get("verified")), None)

Add a test alongside the OAuth cases in apps/backend/tests/test_sec10_auth_controls.py that stubs `/user/emails` with `[{"email": "ops@corp.com", "primary": True, "verified": False}]` and asserts a 400 rather than a session redirect.

title: OAuth/OIDC sign-in links to any existing account by email alone, skips MFA, and ignores registration_open
reasoning:
I tried to find the guard elsewhere in the call path and there is none. Traced the full path for all three callbacks (github_callback:670, google_callback:779, oidc_callback:914) — each calls `_upsert_oauth_user`, then `_bootstrap_redirect_or_none` (returns None once `cfg.auth_enabled` is True, i.e. after OOBE), then `_issue_jwt_and_redirect`. The routes carry only `@limiter.limit(get_limit("auth"))`; no dependency, middleware or type constraint runs any account-resolution check.

Three separate gaps confirmed by reading, not inference:

1. Link-by-email with no provider binding check. `_upsert_oauth_user:385` is `db.query(User).filter(User.email == email).first()`, and the else-branch at :401-412 does `user.provider = provider` — it *overwrites* the binding rather than comparing it. `User.provider` (models.py:1971, default `"local"`) is therefore never used as an authorization input. No `email_verified` claim is checked anywhere: `grep -rn "email_verified" apps/backend/src` returns nothing, and neither `google_callback` (:763) nor `oidc_callback` (:898) inspects it. GitHub is worse in one spot — :651-652 falls back to `emails[0]["email"]` when no primary+verified address exists.

2. MFA is not enforced. `_issue_jwt_and_redirect:425-441` calls `_make_token` → `create_token` (core/security.py:322-345), which stamps only `user_id/exp/aud=SESSION_AUDIENCE/role/scopes`. There is no MFA claim, and `grep -rn "mfa" core/security.py middleware/*.py` finds nothing — so nothing downstream can re-impose it. The password path does enforce it (auth.py:326-343 returns a 5-minute `cb:mfa-challenge` token instead of a session). The OAuth path never reads `user.mfa_enabled`.

3. `registration_open` is ignored. auth.py:145 gates `POST /auth/register` with it; `_upsert_oauth_user`'s is_new branch has no equivalent, and `is_new` is discarded by all three callers (`user, is_new = ...`, never read). docs/settings.md:126 says the setting decides "whether anyone can create an account, or whether new users must be invited" — the OAuth path breaks that contract. The invite plumbing exists and is correct (`consume_invite_for_oauth`, user_service.py:333, enforces case-insensitive email match) but `invite_token` is `Query(None)` and its absence is not an error.

Reachability with shipped config: docs/auth-access.md:124 calls generic OIDC "the recommended option for homelabs" and walks through Authentik. Keycloak ships with realm "Verify Email" off and Authentik supports self-enrollment, so a low-privileged IdP user editing their own profile email to the operator's admin address is not an exotic configuration — they then hit `/api/v1/auth/oauth/oidc/{slug}`, get bound to the existing admin row at :385, and receive a full admin session at :438 with TOTP never requested. docs/auth-access.md's own Security Notes tell operators to "Enable MFA for admin accounts", which this silently defeats. The threat model (docs/security/threat-model.md) covers OIDC only as an SSRF surface; nothing in the residual-risk register R1-R12 accepts this.

Where the auditor overreached: `_is_user_accessible` (core/security.py:401) is not in this file at all, but they conceded that themselves and it does cover the inactive/locked cases on subsequent requests. Google's `email` is in practice provider-verified, so variant 1 is weak there, and GitHub's `emails[0]` fallback only fires for an account with no primary verified address. The generic-OIDC path is where the takeover is real. I raise severity from medium to high rather than lowering it: gaps 2 and 3 hold unconditionally the moment any provider is enabled, and gap 1's outcome is full admin compromise.

No test covers any of this. Only `test_sec10_auth_controls.py` touches this module, and solely for state single-use (:169), state expiry (:191) and SSRF (:235-260); `grep -rln "_upsert_oauth_user"` across `apps/backend/tests` returns nothing.
fix:
Three minimal changes, all in apps/backend/src/app/api/auth_oauth.py.

(a) `_upsert_oauth_user` (:375) — normalize the email the way the password path does (auth.py:304 `.strip().lower()`), gate creation, and refuse a cross-provider link. Add an `invited: bool` keyword so the invite path stays open:

    def _upsert_oauth_user(db, email, display_name, provider, oauth_tokens,
                           avatar_url=None, role="viewer", *, invited: bool = False):
        from app.services.settings_service import get_or_create_settings
        cfg = get_or_create_settings(db)
        email = email.strip().lower()
        user = db.query(User).filter(User.email == email).first()
        is_new = user is None
        if is_new:
            if cfg.auth_enabled and not invited and not getattr(cfg, "registration_open", True):
                raise HTTPException(403, "Registration is currently closed")
            ...
        else:
            # Reuse an existing row only when it is already bound to this provider,
            # or when the sign-in carried an invite for this address. A local row is
            # not implicitly linkable — that is the account-takeover path.
            if cfg.auth_enabled and not invited and user.provider != provider:
                raise HTTPException(403, "This email is already registered. Ask an administrator to link it.")
            ...

The `cfg.auth_enabled` escape keeps the pre-OOBE first-admin flow (`_bootstrap_redirect_or_none`, :465) working unchanged. Pass `invited=bool(_invite_token)` from all three callers (:670, :779, :914).

(b) Reject an unverified email at the source, next to the existing "did not return email" checks. In `oidc_callback` after :900 and `google_callback` after :765:

    if userinfo.get("email_verified") is False:
        raise HTTPException(400, "OIDC provider reported an unverified email")

and in `github_callback` drop the `emails[0]` fallback at :651-652 so only a primary+verified address is accepted.

(c) `_issue_jwt_and_redirect` (:425) — honour MFA using the token format auth.py:334-341 already mints and `/auth/mfa/verify` already redeems:

    if getattr(user, "mfa_enabled", False):
        mfa_token = jwt.encode(
            {"user_id": user.id, "aud": "cb:mfa-challenge",
             "exp": datetime.now(UTC) + timedelta(minutes=5)},
            cfg.jwt_secret or "", algorithm="HS256")
        resp = RedirectResponse(url=f"{base_url}/?cb_mfa_token={mfa_token}", status_code=302)
        resp.headers["Cache-Control"] = "no-store"
        return resp   # no session cookie, no record_session

Add `cb_mfa_token` to the uvicorn access-log scrub list alongside `cb_auth_code` (docs/security/threat-model.md:212 documents that filter), and have LoginPage.jsx feed it to the existing `authApi.mfaVerify(mfaToken, code)` call it already uses for `requires_mfa`.

title: Four discovery write routes have no write authorization — `require_write_auth` passed as a bare default instead of `Depends(...)`
reasoning:
Confirmed by direct inspection of the live router, not just by reading source.

1. `require_write_auth` (core/security.py:569) is a plain `async def`, NOT a `params.Depends` factory. This is the trap: sibling gates `require_role` (rbac.py:137) and `require_scope` (rbac.py:205) DO return `cast(params.Depends, Depends(_dep))`, so the adjacent, correct `user: User = require_role("admin")` at discovery.py:995 is bare-by-design and looks identical to the four broken lines.

2. Empirical check against the repo's pinned FastAPI 0.135.1: `def bad(_user=require_write_auth)` returns 200; `def good(_user=Depends(require_write_auth))` returns 403. The bare form is emitted in OpenAPI as `{"name":"_user","in":"query","required":false}`.

3. Verified on the real imported router (`app.api.discovery`), inspecting `route.dependant`:
   /jobs/{job_id}/batch-import      DEPS=[require_scope._dep, get_db]  QUERY=['_user']
   /jobs/{job_id}/import-as-network DEPS=[require_scope._dep, get_db]  QUERY=['_user']
   /lldp-enrich                     DEPS=[require_scope._dep, get_db]  QUERY=['_user']
   /lldp-jobs/{job_id}/apply        DEPS=[require_scope._dep, get_db]  QUERY=['_user']
   /results/bulk-merge              DEPS=[require_scope._dep, require_role._dep, get_db]
   The correctly-gated sibling carries require_role; the four do not.

4. Only surviving gates are router-level `require_scope("read","*")` (discovery.py:76) and `Depends(require_auth)` at mount (main.py:1727). `ROLE_DEFAULT_SCOPES` grants viewer and demo `read:*`, so `has_scope(scopes,"read","*")` is True for both — a read-only principal passes.

5. Reachable in a default deployment: `POST /api/v1/auth/demo` (api/auth.py:224) is unauthenticated, gated only on `cfg.jwt_secret` existing, and mints a `role="demo"`, `scopes=["read:*"]` bearer token. CSRFMiddleware only enforces when a `cb_session` cookie is present, so a bearer token bypasses it. WriteAdmissionMiddleware is a health/`writes_permitted` gate, not authorization. Nothing else in the path checks a write role.

6. No existing test covers it, and the SEC-3 gate structurally cannot: tests/test_endpoint_policy_inventory.py only asserts that SOME member of `_AUTH_DEPENDENCIES` is present, and the checked-in src/app/security/endpoint_inventory.json already records all four with `rbac_policy: "declared-role-or-scope"` and a `dependency_calls` list containing neither `require_write_auth` nor `require_role` — identical in shape to the read-only GET /lldp-jobs/{job_id}/results.

Impact confirmed real: batch_import creates/updates Hardware rows; import_as_network creates networks and topology nodes; lldp_apply creates Hardware stubs and HardwareConnection edges; lldp_enrich writes a transient DiscoveryProfile + ScanJob and launches an SNMP scan.

Severity restated on my own judgement as HIGH rather than critical: the demo-session path makes it effectively anonymous-to-write which argues upward, but the blast radius is inventory/topology data plus launching a scan job. It is not a clean arbitrary-SSRF primitive — `lldp_enrich` scans IPs read from existing Hardware rows, and `batch_import` sources IPs from stored ScanResult rows, not from attacker-supplied values. No credential disclosure and no admin escalation.
fix:
In apps/backend/src/app/api/discovery.py, change all four parameters (lines 961, 977, 1063, 1143) from

    _user=require_write_auth,

to

    _user: int | None = Depends(require_write_auth),

matching the convention already used at every other call site in api/ (e.g. topologies.py:131, storage.py:32). `Depends` is already imported at discovery.py:5 and `require_write_auth` at :15, so no import changes are needed.

Then regenerate the security inventory so the reviewed record matches reality — apps/backend/scripts/generate_endpoint_inventory.py rewrites src/app/security/endpoint_inventory.json; the four entries should flip from `rbac_policy: "declared-role-or-scope"` to `"editor-or-admin-or-write-scope"` and gain `app.core.security.require_write_auth` in `dependency_calls`. That JSON is CODEOWNERS-gated (@blkleg), so the change is visible in review.

Hardening so this class cannot recur: tests/test_endpoint_policy_inventory.py currently only checks that some auth dependency exists. Add an assertion there that no APIRoute parameter's default is a bare callable — walk `route.dependant.query_params` (and the raw signature via `inspect.signature(route.endpoint)`) and fail if any default is `callable(...)` and not an instance of `fastapi.params.Depends`. That catches the exact shape of this bug across every router, not just discovery.

title: Zip bomb in docs import: ZIP members are fully decompressed before the per-file size check
reasoning:
Confirmed by tracing the full call path and by measurement; I could not refute it on any upstream guard.

Reachability: docs.router is mounted at /api/v1/docs (main.py:1637) behind router-level require_auth plus endpoint-level require_write_auth. require_write_auth (core/security.py:569) admits role "admin" or "editor", or any principal holding the "write" scope — an ordinary editor, not an admin. The is_zip branch (docs.py:141) triggers on a ".zip" filename OR content_type "application/octet-stream", both fully attacker-chosen, so _parse_zip_entries is trivially entered.

No upstream guard exists. main.py registers CORS, CSRF, LegacyToken, Logging, WriteAdmission, SecurityHeaders, TenantRateLimit, Tenant and HttpMetrics middleware; none inspects body or decompressed size. The only cap anywhere is nginx client_max_body_size 10m (docker/nginx.mono.conf:43,99 and deploy/nginx/*.conf), which bounds the COMPRESSED upload — precisely what a compression bomb exploits. Starlette's UploadFile spooling is irrelevant since data is already bounded at 10 MB by nginx.

The bug itself is exactly as described: line 95 calls zf.read(info), a full in-memory decompression, and only line 96 tests len(md_bytes) against _MAX_IMPORT_MD_BYTES. ZipInfo.file_size — the declared uncompressed size, available from the central directory before any read — is never consulted.

Measured, not assumed: a ZIP of zeros built with stdlib ZIP_DEFLATED compresslevel=9 gives a 1028:1 ratio (200 MiB -> 203,954 bytes), so nginx's 10 MB ceiling permits roughly 10 GB uncompressed. Under tracemalloc, zf.read(info) on a ~300 KB member peaked at 601 MB (2x the payload, from buffer growth), while zf.open(info).read(cap+1) peaked at 2.6 MB.

Impact is worse than the auditor stated under the shipped default config. docker-compose.yml:57-63 caps the entire mono container at 2 GB, and that cgroup also hosts postgres, pgbouncer, redis, nats, nginx and six workers (supervisord.mono.conf). uvicorn runs --workers 2 (supervisord.mono.conf:110). Given the 2x peak, roughly 1 GB of uncompressed content — reachable with a ~1 MB ZIP, well under the nginx limit — already drives the cgroup to its ceiling, putting the co-resident database at risk of the cgroup OOM killer. autorestart=true brings the API worker back, but the request is repeatable at will.

Test coverage: none. grep -rn "docs/import\|_parse_zip_entries\|import_docs" over apps/backend/tests/ returns nothing, and no test_docs*.py exists in the repo outside .venv.

Additional variant the auditor did not name, which is why a total budget is required and not merely nice to have: even with a correct per-member file_size check, ~10,000 members of 999 KB each individually pass the 1 MB test while summing to ~10 GB, and that ZIP still compresses under 10 MB. The unbounded member count is also real — each surviving entry becomes a separate create_doc INSERT in docs_service.import_docs (docs_service.py:135-141) inside one request.

Severity high rather than critical only because it requires an authenticated editor-or-above principal; it is a single-request, whole-appliance denial of service against a cgroup containing the database, with no mitigating control anywhere in the path.
fix:
In apps/backend/src/app/api/docs.py, add two constants beside the existing ones (near line 23):

    _MAX_IMPORT_ZIP_ENTRIES = 500
    _MAX_IMPORT_TOTAL_MD_BYTES = 20 * 1024 * 1024  # 20 MB uncompressed across all members

Then in _parse_zip_entries, cap the member count and check the declared size before decompressing, reading through a bounded stream:

    infos = zf.infolist()
    if len(infos) > _MAX_IMPORT_ZIP_ENTRIES:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=413, detail="ZIP must contain ≤ 500 files")

    entries: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
    total_bytes = 0
    for info in infos:
        if info.is_dir() or not info.filename.lower().endswith(".md"):
            continue
        # Prevent path traversal — keep only the bare filename
        safe_name = Path(info.filename).name
        if not safe_name:
            continue
        # Reject on the declared uncompressed size *before* decompressing, so a
        # compression bomb cannot allocate gigabytes ahead of the size check.
        if info.file_size > _MAX_IMPORT_MD_BYTES:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=413, detail=f"{safe_name} exceeds 1 MB limit")
        total_bytes += info.file_size
        if total_bytes > _MAX_IMPORT_TOTAL_MD_BYTES:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=413, detail="ZIP contents exceed 20 MB uncompressed")
        # Read one byte past the cap so a lying central-directory header cannot
        # beat the check above.
        with zf.open(info) as fh:
            md_bytes = fh.read(_MAX_IMPORT_MD_BYTES + 1)
        if len(md_bytes) > _MAX_IMPORT_MD_BYTES:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=413, detail=f"{safe_name} exceeds 1 MB limit")
        title = Path(safe_name).stem or _DEFAULT_IMPORT_TITLE
        entries.append((title, md_bytes.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")))

The bounded zf.open(...).read(cap + 1) is load-bearing rather than defensive extra: info.file_size is attacker-declared, so a header claiming 100 bytes over a 10 GB deflate stream would pass a file_size-only test. Verified under tracemalloc that this form peaks at 2.6 MB where zf.read peaked at 601 MB. 413 with a "≤" detail string matches the existing style at lines 81 and 112. Worth adding a test at apps/backend/tests/api/test_docs.py asserting POST /api/v1/docs/import returns 413 for a deflate bomb, since the endpoint currently has no tests at all.

title: IPAM network scan materialises the full host list before the size check — unbounded hang on IPv6, multi-GB spike on IPv4
reasoning:
Confirmed; I could not refute it. Line 207 is `hosts = list(network.hosts())` and the bound `if len(hosts) > 1022` is on line 208 — strictly after full materialisation.

No upstream guard exists on this path. `NetworkBase.validate_cidr` (schemas/networks.py:12-21) only wraps `ipaddress.ip_network(..., strict=False)` in a try/except for parseability, with no size test. `NetworkUpdate` (schemas/networks.py:33-44) is a bare BaseModel, not a NetworkBase subclass, so it carries no cidr validator at all. `networks_service.create_network` (line 220-236) assigns payload.cidr directly to the model, and `Network.cidr` is `mapped_column(String)` (db/models.py:965) with no length or check constraint. `discovery_network._validate_cidr` / `_MAX_CIDR_ADDRESSES` (services/discovery_network.py:110-132) is imported only by discovery_service.py:775 and never touches this path — and at 1,048,576 addresses its bound is three orders of magnitude looser than 1022 anyway.

Reachable in default configuration through the shipped UI: mounted at /api/v1/ipam (main.py:1944-1946), with a Scan button at IPAddressesTab.jsx:237 fed by a network-picker dropdown via useIPAMData.js:67 -> client.jsx:539. `require_write_auth` (core/security.py:569-588) admits any editor role or any principal holding a write scope — not admin-gated. No test under apps/backend/tests references `ipam/scan` or `scan_network_addresses`. No mitigating timeout: docker/nginx.conf sets `proxy_read_timeout 3600s`, and a client disconnect cannot interrupt a synchronous `def` endpoint holding an anyio threadpool worker.

Measured on this machine: 1M IPv4Address objects cost 0.43s and 109 MB RSS, extrapolating to ~7.2s and ~1.8 GB for a 10.0.0.0/8 record — all spent before returning the 400 that says the range is too large. `ip_network('2001:db8::/32').hosts()` is a generator over 7.9e28 addresses, so `list()` never returns and RSS grows until the worker is OOM-killed.

I would sharpen one point in the report: the IPv6 case needs no hostile CIDR. The standard IPv6 LAN prefix is a /64 (1.8e19 hosts), so an operator recording an ordinary IPv6 subnet and clicking Scan hits the same unbounded hang. The bug fires on intended usage, not only on abuse.

Severity high rather than critical: it wedges a worker permanently and OOM-kills the container, but requires an authenticated editor-or-above and is availability-only — no data loss or auth bypass.

Adjacent, out of scope for this finding: services/bulk_suggest.py:323 has the same `list(net.hosts())[0]` shape guarded only by `net.num_addresses > 1`.
fix:
Test the O(1) integer `num_addresses` before expanding the generator, retaining the existing `len` check so the accept/reject boundary is bit-for-bit unchanged (an IPv4 /22 has num_addresses 1024 / 1022 hosts, so nothing currently accepted becomes rejected). Replace lines 207-209 with:

    if network.num_addresses > 1024:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="CIDR too large (max /22 = 1022 hosts)")

    hosts = list(network.hosts())
    if len(hosts) > 1022:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="CIDR too large (max /22 = 1022 hosts)")

This caps materialisation at 1024 address objects for any input. Add a regression test asserting that POST /api/v1/ipam/scan/{id} on a network whose cidr is "2001:db8::/32" returns 400 promptly.

Do not adopt the auditor's second suggestion of reusing `_MAX_CIDR_ADDRESSES` inside `NetworkBase.validate_cidr` as part of this fix: at 1,048,576 it would not prevent this OOM, and tightening the persisted-CIDR bound to /22 would reject legitimate inventory records for large networks. Giving `NetworkUpdate` a `cidr` validator is a real but separate gap worth its own change.

title: Manual telemetry poll blocks the API event loop for up to ~105s on an unreachable SNMP device
reasoning:
Verified rather than assumed. `poll_now` is `async def` (line 86) and calls the fully synchronous `poll_hardware` (integrations/dispatcher.py:34) at line 98 with no await and no thread hop, so it executes directly on the uvicorn event loop. I checked the refutation paths and none hold: there is no custom APIRoute/route_class or run_in_threadpool anywhere in apps/backend/src/app, so FastAPI does not offload the coroutine; no dependency in the chain (router-level require_auth, require_role("admin"), get_db, get_vault) offloads it either; and the `snmp` package IS installed in both images (Dockerfile:57, Dockerfile.mono:117), so the subprocess calls do not fast-fail with FileNotFoundError.

Worst case is worse than reported. Against a dark host, SNMPNetworkDeviceClient.poll runs 3 snmpget (timeout=5) plus snmpwalk (timeout=10) for CPU, mem_used, mem_size, ifDescr, ifOperStatus, and then BOTH the HC and 32-bit fallback walks for in and out — `_snmp_walk(OID_IF_HC_IN) or _snmp_walk(OID_IF_IN)` falls through because the first returns empty. That is 15 + 50 + 40 = ~105s, not the 85s claimed. subprocess timeouts bound the child process, not the loop.

Reachable in a default deployment: the endpoint is mounted at main.py:1703 and 1709, exposed in the shipped UI via TelemetryPanel.jsx:124,139 -> client.jsx:456, and carries no rate limit (`@limiter.limit` appears only on get_telemetry at line 41). docker/supervisord.mono.conf:110 runs `uvicorn --workers 2`, so two concurrent polls stall the entire API including WebSocket frames.

Not covered by tests: tests/integration/test_telemetry.py:62 monkeypatches `app.api.telemetry.poll_hardware` with an instant synchronous lambda, which pins the current blocking shape rather than detecting it.

The project already has the correct pattern at workers/telemetry_collector.py:100-102, which wraps the identical call in `asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.to_thread(poll_hardware, ...), timeout=timeout_s)` with `timeout_s = max(5, int(os.environ.get("CB_TELEMETRY_DEVICE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS", "20")))` (line 208). These are the only two call sites of poll_hardware; the interactive one never got the guard.

Two errors in the report, neither changing the verdict: (1) there is no ICMP probing on this path, only SNMP subprocesses and synchronous requests, so the title's "ICMP" is wrong; (2) ilo/idrac are not "equally blocking" — ILOClient._get raises ConnectionError on the first failed call (ilo.py:45, timeout=10) and IDRACClient uses timeout=3, so those profiles stall ~10s / ~3s, not 85s. The snmp_network_device profile is the severe case.

I also confirmed the fix is safe: running poll_hardware in a thread makes dispatcher._fire_and_forget_publish take its `asyncio.get_running_loop()` RuntimeError branch and skip the Redis publish, but that is redundant here because write_telemetry (services/telemetry_service.py:216,221) performs cache_telemetry and publish_telemetry itself — which is exactly what the existing test asserts. The collector already runs under this same condition.

Severity high rather than the usual discount for an admin-gated endpoint: this is not an attack requiring a malicious actor. Clicking "Poll now" on a device that appears down is the normal operational use of the button, and that is precisely the input that produces the ~105s stall. require_role("admin") limits who can trigger it, not how long it blocks.

title: get_redis() treats Redis pool exhaustion as a dead server and calls aclose(), disconnecting every live pub/sub socket in the process
reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The mechanism is confirmed both by reading the pinned library and by running it against the local dev Redis with the exact pinned version (redis-py 7.3.0, per apps/backend/requirements.txt:77).

Verified facts:

1. `_try_connect` (redis.py:80-86) builds the single process-wide client via `from_url(..., max_connections=20)`. `Redis.from_url` sets `auto_close_connection_pool = True` (asyncio/client.py), so `aclose()` calls `connection_pool.disconnect()`, and the async `ConnectionPool.disconnect(inuse_connections=True)` default disconnects in-use connections too (asyncio/connection.py:1416-1432).

2. `r.pubsub()` binds to that same pool and takes one connection on `subscribe()`, holding it until teardown (`PubSub.connect` -> `self.connection = await self.connection_pool.get_connection()`). Every long-lived listener does exactly that: ws_telemetry.py:101, ws_monitors.py:113, ws_discovery.py:120, ws_agents.py:986, and agent_registry.py:1402 via `claim_agent_control_frames`, which IS wired in production — `_run_control_frame_listener` is started per /link socket at ws_agents.py:709, so every connected agent permanently holds one pool connection.

3. `get_available_connection` raises `MaxConnectionsError("Too many connections")` (asyncio/connection.py:1370), and `MaxConnectionsError` subclasses `ConnectionError` (exceptions.py:267), so it is swallowed by the bare `except Exception` at redis.py:127 — the branch written for a dead server.

Live reproduction (scratchpad repro2.py, poetry venv with redis 7.3.0, against circuitbreaker-redis-1):
  in_use 20 / all 20 pubsub conns in pool._in_use_connections / connected before: 20
  PING RAISED MaxConnectionsError
  connected after aclose: 0
  sub0 message: None   (a message published right after the flush is lost)
So the 20th subscriber is enough: the next `get_redis()` ping raises, the except branch calls `aclose()` (line 130), and every live pub/sub socket in the process is severed at once.

Reachability with shipped defaults: docs/operations/sizing-profiles.md:37 lists **Medium = 50 agents, 5 concurrent users as a supported profile**, and docker/supervisord.mono.conf:110 runs 2 uvicorn workers (deploy/systemd runs 1). 50 agents over 2 workers is ~25 long-lived pub/sub connections per worker against a pool of 20 — the supported profile exceeds the hard-coded cap before a single browser tab connects. The WS caps are also far above it (telemetry 100, monitors 100, shared manager 50; agent /link uncapped), and `CB_RUN_INPROCESS_WORKERS=true` (the default) puts the six worker programs on the same pool. Nothing in the sizing doc budgets the Redis pool — it budgets only the SQLAlchemy pool.

Where the auditor overstates, and where the real harm is:
- Overstated: it is not a permanent teardown of every stream. I verified (repro3.py) that each PubSub transparently reconnects and re-subscribes on its next `get_message`, and the replacement client gets a *fresh* pool that the old subscribers no longer count against — so it does not immediately re-enter exhaustion. The real steady-state behaviour is a recurring flush: roughly every 20 newly-established long-lived subscribers, every current subscriber's Redis socket is dropped and re-established, losing every pub/sub message published in that window (pub/sub has no replay — including agent control frames: update, disconnect, key.rotate) and breaking any command in flight on those connections.
- Overstated: `get_redis()` returning `None` for 10 s is not the normal outcome — the first failure usually passes the cooldown gate and reconnects within the same call.
- Understated: when a *second* exhaustion lands inside the 10 s cooldown — exactly what a burst of agent reconnects after a backend restart produces — `get_redis()` returns `None` at line 137, and the listeners that receive `None` never retry. `ws_telemetry._redis_listener` does `await stop_event.wait()`, so that socket stays open, keeps answering keep-alives, and silently delivers zero frames for its entire life. `claim_agent_control_frames` returns immediately (`if r is None: return`), so `_run_control_frame_listener`'s `async for` ends cleanly without even a `record_stream_fault` — leaving a /link connection accepting heartbeats it can never answer with a control frame, which is precisely the failure the comment at ws_agents.py:507-517 says was hardened against.

No guard exists anywhere on the path: no `CB_REDIS_MAX_CONNECTIONS`, no BlockingConnectionPool, no separate pub/sub pool, no accounting of subscribers against the cap, and no test covers core/redis.py's pool behaviour (there is no tests/**/ *redis* module for it). Severity is high rather than critical: it degrades the real-time plane, not the Postgres source of truth, it self-heals in the single-flush case, and it needs ~20 concurrent long-lived subscribers — but it is silent, process-wide, and reachable at a documented supported scale with default configuration.
fix:
Two changes in apps/backend/src/app/core/redis.py.

1. Never let a local resource shortage disconnect healthy connections. Add the import and a dedicated branch ahead of the generic one in `get_redis()`:

    from redis.exceptions import MaxConnectionsError

    if _redis is not None:
        try:
            await cast(Awaitable[Any], _redis.ping())
            return _redis
        except MaxConnectionsError:
            # Pool exhaustion is a local shortage, not a dead server. aclose()
            # here would call pool.disconnect(), severing every in-use
            # connection — including the pub/sub socket each WS listener holds
            # for the life of its connection. Degrade this one call instead.
            _logger.warning(
                "Redis pool exhausted (max_connections=%d) — degrading this call",
                _MAX_CONNECTIONS,
            )
            return None
        except Exception:
            ...unchanged...

(`MaxConnectionsError` exists in the pinned redis==7.3.0; if the `>=5.0.0` floor in pyproject.toml must keep working, guard the import with a try/except ImportError fallback to `redis.exceptions.ConnectionError`.)

2. Size the pool from the subscriber population instead of a literal, following the module's existing env convention:

    _MAX_CONNECTIONS: int = int(os.environ.get("CB_REDIS_MAX_CONNECTIONS", "250"))
    ...
    max_connections=_MAX_CONNECTIONS,

250 covers the shipped WS caps (telemetry 100 + monitors 100 + shared manager 50) plus the agent /link sockets and command traffic, per worker. Add the row to the "Application connection pool" table in docs/operations/sizing-profiles.md so the Redis pool is budgeted alongside the DB pool.

Optional follow-up (not needed to close the defect): build pub/sub on its own `ConnectionPool` so subscribers can never starve the command path — that removes the coupling rather than just widening it.

title: Nightly full-state snapshot job is only registered by discovery-profile writes, never at boot
reasoning:
Confirmed by tracing every registration site. `scheduler.add_job(_run_scheduled_snapshot, CronTrigger(hour=2, minute=0), id="daily_db_snapshot")` at scheduler.py:156-161 is the only registration of that job anywhere in the tree (repo-wide grep for `daily_db_snapshot` and `_run_scheduled_snapshot` hits only core/scheduler.py). It sits inside `reload_discovery_jobs()`, whose only callers are write handlers: api/discovery.py:472,546 (profile create/update), api/agents.py:1071,1544, and services/discovery_profiles_service.py:259,378,445. There is no boot caller.

I enumerated all 26 `id="..."` job registrations in main.py's lifespan (lines 854-1346): purge_old_scan_results, audit_log_purge, monitor_probe_run_purge, audit_partition_maintenance, disable_expired_demo_users, expire_pending_agents, daily_uptime_rollup, audit_spool_drain, pg_backup, integration_sync_job, cve_sync, privacy_periodic, discovery_reconciler, agent_discovery_reconcile, refresh_ip_pool, docker_topology_sync, proxmox_*, arp_prober, cert_auto_renewal, vault_rotation_check, analytics_job, retention_job. `daily_db_snapshot` is absent. The boot path's only discovery-related call is `_register_discovery_profile_crons(scheduler, sched_db)` (main.py:1101), which registers per-profile crons and nothing else.

Consequences, both reachable with stock config: (a) an install that never edits a discovery profile or agent never registers the 02:00 snapshot at all; (b) even an install that has edited one loses the job on every process restart until the next profile write, because `reload_discovery_jobs` also `job.remove()`s and re-adds this set. The codebase already recognises this exact hazard one screen away — main.py:1070 documents that `agent_discovery_reconcile` was deliberately moved into the lifespan because "a job added there is silently unregistered the next time an administrator saves a profile" — and tests/services/test_agent_discovery_reconcile.py:848 enforces it for the reconciler only. No test asserts `daily_db_snapshot` exists.

The gap is invisible from the outside: `_run_scheduled_snapshot` swallows BackupError and Exception into log lines (scheduler.py:83-87), and `latest_backup_info()` (services/db_backup.py:99) globs `cb-*.sql.gz` — the artifact of the *registered* `pg_backup` job — so the backup readout looks healthy while no `cb-snapshot-*.tar.gz` is ever produced.

Two corrections to the auditor. First, the reported line 126 is stale (concurrent churn); the add_job is at 156-161. Second, the tail of the suggested fix is wrong: `SingleOwnerScheduler.add_job` (scheduler.py:31-37) wraps every job in `job_lock.single_owner`, a pg advisory lock keyed by job id, precisely so `uvicorn --workers 2` (docker/supervisord.mono.conf:110) runs it once — the "two tarfile.open on the same path" corruption cannot occur, and `max_instances=1` is already APScheduler's default. Only the relocation is needed.

Severity high rather than critical: the nightly `pg_backup` dump is registered and still runs, and operators retain manual `POST /admin/db/snapshot` (api/admin_db.py:170) and `cb snapshot` (cli.py:833). But the snapshot is the only artifact carrying the vault key, uploads and config, and since the key can auto-rotate into data/.env (vault_service.load_vault_key), the surviving .sql.gz can be undecryptable on its own.
fix:
Move the registration out of `reload_discovery_jobs` into the lifespan, following the `agent_discovery_reconcile` precedent exactly.

1. Delete scheduler.py:155-161 (the `# Daily full-state snapshot at 02:00` block). Keep `_run_scheduled_snapshot` where it is — it is the job body, not the registration.

2. In apps/backend/src/app/main.py, immediately after the `pg_backup` block (line ~1004), add:

    # Daily full-state snapshot at 02:00 — the tarball that carries the vault
    # key, uploads and config, and the only artifact `cb restore` accepts.
    # Registered here rather than in `core.scheduler.reload_discovery_jobs`,
    # which first removes every job it registered: a snapshot job added there
    # exists only between an administrator's profile write and the next
    # restart, and `latest_backup_info()` reads the pg_backup artifact, so
    # nothing surfaces the gap until restore time.
    from app.core.scheduler import _run_scheduled_snapshot

    scheduler.add_job(
        _run_scheduled_snapshot,
        trigger=CronTrigger(hour=2, minute=0),
        id="daily_db_snapshot",
        replace_existing=True,
        misfire_grace_time=3600,
    )

(`misfire_grace_time=3600` matches `daily_uptime_rollup`/`discovery_purge` and lets a restart that straddles 02:00 still take the snapshot; without it APScheduler's default silently drops the missed run. Do not add `max_instances=1` or temp-file/os.replace juggling — `SingleOwnerScheduler` already guarantees one runner per job id.)

Consider renaming `_run_scheduled_snapshot` to `run_scheduled_snapshot` since it now has a cross-module caller.

3. Add a regression test beside the existing precedent in apps/backend/tests/services/, mirroring `test_the_interval_job_is_registered_in_the_lifespan_and_not_in_reload_discovery_jobs`:

    def test_the_snapshot_job_is_registered_in_the_lifespan_and_not_in_reload_discovery_jobs():
        backend = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
        main_py = (backend / "src/app/main.py").read_text()
        scheduler_py = (backend / "src/app/core/scheduler.py").read_text()
        assert 'id="daily_db_snapshot"' in main_py
        assert 'id="daily_db_snapshot"' not in scheduler_py

title: Service-account JWTs (user_id=0) are accepted on signature alone — deleting or rotating the APIToken row does not revoke them
reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not; every candidate guard is absent.

Path traced end to end:
1. `POST /api/v1/auth/service-account` (api/auth.py:478-533) is the only caller of `create_token()` that passes `user_id=0` (the other three call sites — auth.py:255 demo, admin_users.py:470 masquerade, auth_service.py:276 login — all pass a real `user.id`). It mints a self-contained HS256 JWT carrying `scopes` and `exp` of 8760h (1 year) when `expires_at` is omitted, and stores only `create_salted_api_token_hash(token)` in `api_tokens`, docstring: "for tracking and revocation".
2. `resolve_optional_user_id_sync` (core/security.py:465-...) is the single auth resolver behind `get_optional_user` → `require_auth_always` / `require_write_auth` / `require_role` / `require_scope`. For that JWT it: (a) `_is_legacy_admin` false, (b) `is_session_revoked` finds nothing — `record_session` returns early for `user.id == 0` (services/user_service.py:41), so no `user_sessions` row exists to match, (c) `jwt.decode` succeeds, `uid_raw == 0`, (d) `_is_user_accessible(db, 0)` returns `True` unconditionally (:401-403), (e) scopes are taken from the JWT claim and the function returns at :518. The `db.query(APIToken).all()` scan at :527 is unreachable for these tokens — it sits after the `return`/`except` fallthrough and is only reached when JWT decode fails. So the `APIToken` row, including its own `expires_at`, is never consulted.
3. Downstream, uid 0 with `*:*` (the shipped `full_access` preset) is `_service_user()` — `role="admin"`, `is_superuser=True` — in both `require_role` (core/rbac.py:177) and `require_scope` (:216). So a "revoked" token retains admin, including the right to call `/auth/service-account` again and mint fresh credentials.
4. `DELETE /api/v1/auth/api-tokens/{id}` (api/auth.py:639-655) deletes the row and calls `invalidate_token_cache()`, which only does `_session_cache.clear()` (core/security.py:177-186). Clearing the cache just forces a re-decode, which succeeds. Net effect: zero.
5. `POST /api/v1/auth/api-tokens/{id}/rotate` (api/auth.py:659-694) mints `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` — an opaque string — for a credential whose real form is a JWT, deletes the old row, and leaves the old JWT valid. The UI (apps/frontend/src/components/settings/AccessTokensManager.jsx:109) then toasts "Token rotated. The previous secret no longer works." That is false for service-account rows, and the same manager is what creates them (`is_service_account` is a first-class field, tests/api/test_api_tokens_admin.py:54).
6. No middleware closes it: `middleware/legacy_token.py` only rejects `CB_API_TOKEN`; csrf/tenant/rate-limit/security-headers/logging never touch `api_tokens`. There is no jti/denylist anywhere in the backend.
7. `apps/backend/src/app/api/ws_monitors.py:244-265` repeats the identical shape for the monitor WebSocket: `uid == 0` short-circuits to a superuser reader snapshot before its own `APIToken` scan at :272.
8. Tests: `tests/api/test_token_scopes.py` covers empty-scope denial and unknown-scope rejection; `tests/api/test_api_tokens_admin.py` covers revoke/rotate only against opaque-token rows created via `create_salted_api_token_hash("raw-<label>")`. Nothing asserts that a revoked or rotated *service-account* token stops authenticating.

Reachability in a default deployment: yes. Requires only `auth_enabled` + `jwt_secret` (post-bootstrap normal state) and an admin having created a service account — which docs/metrics.md:33-61, docs/deployment-security.md:40 and docs/installation/configuration.md:19-20 all actively push as the supported replacement for the deprecated `CB_API_TOKEN`. docs/reference/api.md:43 explicitly claims these tokens "support expiry, rotation and revocation".

Severity high, not critical: it grants no new access to an unauthenticated attacker and needs a token to have been issued and leaked first. But the failure mode is a revocation control that reports success while doing nothing, on a credential that defaults to one-year `*:*`, with the API-token expiry column silently ignored — the operator's only containment lever for a leaked headless credential is inert.

One correction to the auditor's suggested fix: matching on `create_salted_api_token_hash(jwt)` cannot work — the salt is 32 fresh `os.urandom` bytes per call (core/security.py:51-60), so the stored value is not reproducible. The lookup must scan with `verify_salted_api_token_hash`, as the existing branch at :527 does.
fix:
In `resolve_optional_user_id_sync` (core/security.py), gate the `uid_int == 0` acceptance on a live `APIToken` row before returning the sentinel. Replace the body of the `uid_raw is not None` branch (~:509-519) with:

    uid_raw = payload.get("user_id")
    if uid_raw is not None:
        uid_int = int(uid_raw)
        if uid_int == 0:
            # A service-account JWT is only live while its APIToken row is.
            # Revocation and rotation delete that row; without this the signed
            # JWT would outlive both, up to its own 1-year `exp`.
            from app.db.models import APIToken

            row = next(
                (
                    c
                    for c in db.query(APIToken).all()
                    if verify_salted_api_token_hash(raw_token, c.token_hash or "")
                ),
                None,
            )
            if row is None or (row.expires_at and row.expires_at <= utcnow()):
                return None
            token_scopes = _normalise_token_scopes(payload.get("scopes"))
            _session_cache_set(token_hash, 0, token_scopes)
            _set_request_token_scopes(request, token_scopes)
            return 0
        if _is_user_accessible(db, uid_int):
            _session_cache_set(token_hash, uid_int, None)
            _set_request_token_scopes(request, None)
            return uid_int
        return None

Note the scan must use `verify_salted_api_token_hash`, not `create_salted_api_token_hash` — the salt is per-token random, so there is no direct lookup. The existing 10s `_session_cache` plus `invalidate_token_cache()` on revoke keeps the added scan off the hot path, and it is the same scan opaque tokens already pay for. `_is_legacy_admin` returns at the top of the function, so `CB_LEGACY_AUTH` rollback is unaffected; the pre-bootstrap sentinel also returns earlier.

Mirror the same gate in `apps/backend/src/app/api/ws_monitors.py` at the `if uid == 0:` branch (:244), which has the identical JWT-first short-circuit ahead of its own `APIToken` scan at :272.

Then fix `rotate_api_token` (api/auth.py:659) so a service-account row (`old.label.startswith(_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_LABEL_PREFIX)`) re-mints a JWT rather than an opaque string — `create_token(0, cfg.jwt_secret, hours_until(old.expires_at) or 8760, scopes=list(old.scopes or []), extra_claims={"label": old.label})` — and store `create_salted_api_token_hash` of that JWT on the replacement row, keeping `created_by` semantics unchanged. Without this the rotated secret authenticates through the opaque-token branch as the rotating admin instead of as the service account.

Regression tests worth adding alongside: create a service account, `DELETE` it, assert the token now 401s; rotate it, assert the old token 401s and the new one still carries the original scopes; and assert an `APIToken.expires_at` in the past denies a JWT whose own `exp` is still future.

title: pg_dump output buffered entirely in memory can OOM the 2 GB mono container
reasoning:
Verified and could not refute.

REACHABLE IN DEFAULT CONFIG. core/scheduler.py:155-160 registers `daily_db_snapshot` (CronTrigger hour=2) unconditionally at scheduler start — no enable flag, no setting gate, no size preflight anywhere in db_backup.run_full_snapshot before it calls build_snapshot. docker-compose.yml:57-61 caps the shipped mono container at 2G, and docker/supervisord.mono.conf confirms postgres, pgbouncer, nats, redis, nginx, `uvicorn --workers 2` and seven worker programs share that cgroup. Dockerfile.mono:102-143 installs postgresql-client, so pg_dump is present; note snapshot.py has no `shutil.which("pg_dump")` guard (backup_postgres does).

MEMORY MATH IS WORSE THAN REPORTED. capture_output=True routes through subprocess._communicate, which accumulates read chunks in a list and then b"".join()s them, so peak RSS is ~2x the uncompressed dump at the join, before `raw` is bound at line 92. The auditor's line-95 claim is the one weak part: db_gz_path.read_bytes() reads the COMPRESSED file (~1/10th), not a second full copy. title: Snapshot staging uses the system temp dir, which is a 100 MB tmpfs in the shipped Docker deployment

No existing coverage: `apps/backend/tests/services/test_snapshot.py` never references staging, mkdtemp or CB_DATA_DIR, and runs outside the container where /tmp is a real filesystem, so every test passes regardless.

The codebase already established the correct pattern one module away: `services/certificate_service.py:56-68` `_certbot_tmp_root()` puts scratch under `$CB_DATA_DIR/tmp` precisely because the container root is read-only, with an OSError fallback to `tempfile.gettempdir()`, and `acme_service.py:249` consumes it as `TemporaryDirectory(dir=...)`. `entrypoint-mono.sh:71` already creates `${CB_DATA_DIR}/tmp` on the persistent volume for that helper.         /tmp is a 100 MB tmpfs in the mono container (docker-compose.yml), and the
        staging tree holds the dump plus an uncompressed copy of uploads/. Stage on

title: SSDP listener runs a blocking multi-round-trip DB write per multicast packet on the API event loop, with attacker-defeatable dedup and no retention on listener_events
reasoning:
Confirmed reachable end to end. main.py:1354-1360 launches listener_service.start with asyncio.create_task inside the API lifespan, with no topology gate (unlike the in-process workers a few lines below), so _ssdp_recv_loop runs on the uvicorn event loop. From there _ssdp_recv_loop -> _handle_ssdp_packet -> _record_event is one unbroken await chain with no executor hop, and _record_event line 358 opens a synchronous SessionLocal() against the psycopg engine (db/session.py:46, pool_pre_ping=True plus a set_config on every checkout), then runs a SELECT, an INSERT and a COMMIT. That is roughly five blocking round-trips per datagram executed directly on the loop. The repo's own convention is the opposite -- integrations/proxmox_client.py:4 states "asyncio.to_thread so the FastAPI event loop is never blocked", and core/update_check.py:246, core/job_lock.py:165 and core/retry.py:32 all follow it; this listener is the outlier.

The input is genuinely attacker-controlled and unauthenticated: service_type at line 334 is headers.get("st") or headers.get("nt"), straight from the SSDP frame, and it is half the _DEDUP_WINDOW key, so varying that one header per packet defeats dedup completely and every packet becomes a committed row whose properties_json carries the full attacker-supplied header dict. Any host with L2 adjacency can emit NOTIFY datagrams to 239.255.255.250:1900 at thousands per second at negligible cost; at roughly 1-2 ms of blocking DB time per packet, a low-rate flood saturates the loop and the entire API stops serving. Because loop.sock_recvfrom returns an already-completed future when data is queued, the recv loop does not reliably yield between packets either, which makes the starvation sharper rather than softer.

The retention half checks out too: grep for listener_events / ListenerEvent outside migrations yields only the model, this service, and the read-only endpoint at api/discovery.py:1420. run_retention_executor (services/intelligence/retention.py) covers only HardwareLiveMetric, AgentHostSample and AgentHostSampleHourly, and there is no purge job, row cap or partitioning anywhere, so the flood also fills the disk permanently. The model carries a single index on seen_at (models.py:1936), so the dedup SELECT has no supporting composite index.

Refutations I tried and rejected: (1) listener_enabled defaults to False (models.py:1407, migration server_default "0") -- a genuine mitigation, but it is the opt-in switch for a shipped headline feature surfaced in settings and api/capabilities.py:61, not an exotic config; (2) the stock docker-compose.yml uses bridge networking so LAN multicast would not arrive -- true, and docs/discovery.md:131 says so, but docs/installation/docker-compose.md:109-117 documents network_mode: host, docs/updates/v0.3.3_release.md:28 says enabling LAN discovery auto-generates exactly that override, and every bare-metal path (install.sh, nfpm.yaml packaging, cb-proxmox-deploy.sh) is host-network by construction, so the affected deployment is the intended one for this feature; (3) something upstream throttles -- record_stream_fault (services/stream_faults.py) throttles only log lines on the failure path, and no HTTP middleware or rate limiter is in front of a raw UDP socket. (4) Existing tests -- apps/backend/tests/test_rel07_listener_recovery.py covers socket leak, read-error give-up and NATS publish failure only; nothing covers intake rate, loop blocking or table growth.

One auditor claim I would soften: "each additional row makes the per-packet stall longer" overstates it, because the seen_at index bounds the dedup scan to the 60-second window rather than the whole table. Under a flood that window still holds tens of thousands of rows, so the effect is real but window-scoped. Severity high rather than critical: total API unavailability plus unbounded disk growth from an unauthenticated attacker at near-zero cost, but gated behind an operator enabling the listener and behind L2 adjacency. The mDNS path shares the defect (_handle_mdns_service offloads get_service_info to an executor but then awaits _record_event on the loop), though it is not attacker-amplifiable the same way.
fix:
Three minimal changes, in order of importance.

1. Get the DB work off the loop. Split the body of _record_event's DB block into a sync helper and call it via asyncio.to_thread, matching core/update_check.py:246 and core/job_lock.py:165:

    def _persist_event(source, service_type, name, ip_address, port, properties) -> bool:
        """Sync SQLAlchemy — call via asyncio.to_thread. Returns True if a row was written."""
        db = SessionLocal()
        try:
            cutoff = datetime.now(UTC) - _DEDUP_WINDOW
            if db.query(ListenerEvent).filter(...).first():
                return False
            db.add(ListenerEvent(...)); db.commit(); return True
        except Exception as exc:
            record_stream_fault(f"{_COMPONENT}.record", exc, logger=_logger,
                                context={"source": source, "ip": ip_address},
                                fault=FAULT_DATABASE)
            db.rollback(); return False
        finally:
            db.close()

  then in _record_event: `wrote = await asyncio.to_thread(_persist_event, ...)`, and only publish to NATS when `wrote` is True (that also fixes the current behaviour of publishing nothing on the dedup-hit early return while still publishing after a failed insert). Note FAULT_DATABASE already exists in stream_faults.py for exactly this.

2. Drop flood traffic before it reaches the DB at all. Add a bounded in-process gate in _handle_ssdp_packet keyed on the source IP only — never on header values — e.g. a module-level dict of ip -> (tokens, last_refill) with a small cap (say 5 events/sec burst 10) plus a hard bound on the dict size (evict oldest when it exceeds a few thousand entries, so the gate itself cannot be a memory sink). Packets over budget are counted via record_stream_fault and dropped without a session checkout. This is the piece that actually stops the DoS; to_thread alone just moves the stall into the thread pool.

3. Bound the table. Add a listener_events purge alongside the existing audit_log_purge job (main.py:869 / services/log_purge.py) — an APScheduler CronTrigger job deleting rows older than a retention window (7-14 days is consistent with the telemetry hot window default). While adding the migration for that, also add the composite index on (ip_address, service_type, seen_at) that the dedup filter needs.

Apply the same to_thread treatment to the mDNS path, which shares _record_event.

title: Audit-log retention purge deletes the chain genesis, so verify-chain reports tampering on every install past the retention window
reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. Traced path, all in default configuration:

Chain construction is unconditional and universal. `write_log` (`services/log_service.py:219-222`) sets `previous_hash = last_log.log_hash if last_log else None` and `entry.log_hash = compute_log_hash(entry, previous_hash)`; `audit_spool.drain` (`services/audit_spool.py:137-145`) does the same. The purge is scheduled and enabled by default. `main.py:864-871` registers `purge_old_audit_logs` on `CronTrigger(hour=3, minute=15)` inside the lifespan, before `scheduler.start()` (`main.py:1350`). `AppSettings.audit_log_retention_days` defaults to 90 in the model (`db/models.py:1324`), in the migration (`0017_...:181`), and in the schema (`schemas/settings.py:161`); `docs/security/privacy.md:96` documents 90 days as shipped behaviour. It is the only partial deleter of `Log` rows in the tree (`grep` for `delete(Log)` / `Log.timestamp <` returns only this line plus read-side filters). The other deleter, `clear_logs` in `api/logs.py:265-273`, deletes *every* row, so the follow-up event legitimately becomes a new genesis with `previous_hash = None` — that path is safe and is exactly why this one is not.

4. `verify_audit_chain` (`core/audit_chain.py:141-152`) starts `previous_hash = None` and its first test is `if log.previous_hash != previous_hash`. The earliest surviving row carries the SHA-256 of a deleted row, so it fails immediately and returns after `checked_count = 1`.

Empirically reproduced against the real `compute_log_hash` / `verify_audit_chain` with the real `Log` model (six chained rows, delete rows older than 90 days):
  before purge: {'valid': True, ... 'Chain verified (6 entries).'}
  deleted: 1
  after purge: {'valid': False, 'first_failure_id': 2, 'message': 'Log id=2: previous_hash mismatch (chain broken).', 'checked_count': 1}

No guard exists anywhere in the call path: the purge takes no audit-chain lock, writes no checkpoint, and `admin_audit.py:31` passes the session straight to `verify_audit_chain` with no anchor argument. No test covers the interaction — `tests/integration/test_phase2_audit.py` seeds `Log` rows directly with no hashes at all and never calls the verifier; `apps/backend/tests/test_logs.py:167,202` exercise repair and concurrency but never purge.

Severity high, on my own reading rather than by copying the auditor. It is not an access-control break, and the frontend does not yet call the endpoint (`grep` for `verifyChain` in `apps/frontend/src` is empty; it is still spec-only in `specs/1.0.0/slices/ui-3-audit-view.md`), so no user-facing alarm fires today. The obvious operator response, `POST /audit-log/repair-chain`, rewrites every downstream hash and destroys the real evidence.

One correction to the auditor's suggested fix: its first variant (set the new earliest row's `previous_hash` to NULL and recompute its `log_hash`) is wrong. The verifier compares each row's stored `previous_hash` against the *recomputed* expected hash of the prior row, not the prior row's stored `log_hash`, so changing one row's hash cascades — verification would then fail at the second surviving row instead of the first, and fixing that requires rewriting the whole table, i.e. exactly what `repair_audit_chain` does and exactly the evidence destruction to be avoided.     lock_audit_chain(db)
    last_purged = db.execute(
        select(Log).where(Log.timestamp < cutoff).order_by(Log.id.desc()).limit(1)
    ).scalar_one_or_none()

(If `row is None` no settings row exists yet, which is also the case where the default 90 applies; `get_or_create_settings` may be used instead, matching `log_service.write_log`'s own settings access.)

3. `core/audit_chain.py`: replace the hardcoded genesis seed in `verify_audit_chain` with the stored checkpoint —

    from app.db.models import AppSettings
    settings_row = session.query(AppSettings).first()
    previous_hash: str | None = settings_row.audit_chain_checkpoint_hash if settings_row else None

title: TELEMETRY and DISCOVERY JetStream streams are created with no retention policy or limits
reasoning:
I tried to find a guard and there is none. Traced end to end:

- `_dispatch_telemetry` (line 141) publishes `telemetry.ingest.{hardware_id}` carrying the full raw payload.
- `telemetry_ingest_worker._ensure_stream` line 53 declares the stream that captures it: `js.add_stream(name="TELEMETRY", subjects=["telemetry.ingest.>"])`. nats-py `StreamConfig` defaults apply: `retention=limits`, `max_msgs=-1`, `max_bytes=-1`, `max_age=0`, `storage=file`. Under LimitsPolicy an acked message is NOT removed, and the worker does ack (line 236). So the stream only ever grows.
- `workers/discovery.py:108` has the identical defect for DISCOVERY (lower volume, same class).

NO MITIGATION IN THE MONO IMAGE — this is the part I most expected to refute the finding and it does the opposite. `docker/supervisord.mono.conf:78` launches `nats-server --jetstream --store_dir /data/nats --auth "$NATS_AUTH_TOKEN"` with no config file and no store limits, so JetStream falls back to its default of up to 75% of the filesystem. `/data` also holds `pgdata` (`docker/entrypoint-mono.sh:71`), so this really is unbounded growth on the volume Postgres writes to. `deploy/config/nats.conf:13` does set `max_file_store: 2GB`, but that file is only rendered for the native systemd install (`deploy/setup.sh:734`, `deploy/systemd/circuitbreaker-nats.service:9`) — and there the outcome is merely different, not benign: hitting the 2GB account limit makes every JetStream publish fail account-wide, taking CB_EVENTS, MONITOR_POLL, MONITOR_PROBE and DISCOVERY down with it.

WHERE THE AUDITOR IS SLIGHTLY OFF, and where it is worse than stated:
- The claim "`js_publish` starts failing" is wrong for this path: `_dispatch_telemetry` calls `nats_client.publish` (core NATS, `nats_client.py:168`), not `js_publish`. That makes it worse, not better — a core publish is fire-and-forget, so once the stream cannot store, the server drops the message and the client sees success. The documented "graceful degradation … falls back to direct writes" only triggers on `nats_client.is_connected` being False; NATS-up-but-JetStream-full silently loses telemetry with no error and no fallback.

WORK QUEUE IS SAFE HERE: I checked every publisher and consumer of `telemetry.ingest.>`. Exactly one publisher (`telemetry_collector`) and exactly one consumer (durable `telemetry_ingest`, pull-subscribed on the full `telemetry.ingest.>` filter, line 182). No overlapping filters, so WorkQueuePolicy is valid. Same for DISCOVERY (`discovery.jobs`, single queue-group consumer that acks/naks).

NO TEST COVERS IT. `tests/services/test_monitor_probe_stream.py` pins `retention == RetentionPolicy.WORK_QUEUE` and `max_age` for MONITOR_PROBE, and its own docstring warns that the swallowed "already in use" branch means a later change never reaches a deployed stream. That convention exists in the repo and was simply never applied to these two `add_stream` calls. Nothing purges these streams — every `purge` hit in the tree is a Postgres row purge.

Severity high rather than critical: no attacker involvement, impact accrues over weeks of normal operation rather than on demand, and it is availability/data-loss rather than a security boundary. But it is a real, default-configuration path to disk exhaustion on the Postgres volume, so it is above medium.

Give both streams the same treatment `ensure_monitor_poll_stream` already uses, and add an `update_stream` retrofit so existing deployments are not left with the limitless stream (the "already in use" branch is swallowed at debug level).

In `apps/backend/src/app/workers/telemetry_ingest_worker.py`, replace the `add_stream` call at line 53:

    from nats.js.api import RetentionPolicy

        "subjects": [_SUBJECT_FILTER],
        # WorkQueuePolicy: the ingest worker acks each message, so acked rows are
        # deleted rather than retained forever. max_age bounds the backlog if the
        # worker is down — stale telemetry has no value once it is minutes old.
        "retention": RetentionPolicy.WORK_QUEUE,
        "max_age": int(os.getenv("CB_TELEMETRY_STREAM_MAX_AGE_S", "3600")),
        "max_bytes": int(os.getenv("CB_TELEMETRY_STREAM_MAX_BYTES", str(256 * 1024 * 1024))),
    }
    try:
        await js.add_stream(**_cfg)
        _logger.info("NATS %s stream created", _STREAM_NAME)
    except Exception as exc:
        msg = str(exc).lower()

Apply the same shape at `apps/backend/src/app/workers/discovery.py:108` for DISCOVERY (`retention=RetentionPolicy.WORK_QUEUE` plus a `max_age`; `process_job` acks/naks, so a work queue is correct there too).
