title: Stored `javascript:` URL in service.url renders into an unchecked `href`, executing script in the viewer's session
reasoning:
Confirmed end to end; I could not find any guard in the path.

REACHABLE INPUT: `POST/PATCH /api/v1/services` gates only on `require_write_auth` (apps/backend/src/app/core/security.py:586), which admits role `editor` or any token holding the `write` scope. `ServiceBase.url` / `ServiceUpdate.url` are bare `str | None` with no validator (apps/backend/src/app/schemas/services.py:28 and :51), and `services_service.create_service` persists it verbatim (`url=payload.url`, apps/backend/src/app/services/services_service.py:272). The UI exposes it as a plain text field (`{ name: 'url', label: 'URL' }`, apps/frontend/src/pages/ServicesPage.jsx:334) and as an inline-editable column (line 505), so no API scripting is even required.

SINK: `<a href={service.url} target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">` at ServiceDetail.jsx:200, where `service` is the DB-backed prop passed from ServicesPage. `target="_blank"`/`rel="noreferrer"` are irrelevant to a `javascript:` URI, which runs in the current document. The same DB string reaches a second sink at HardwareDetail.jsx:585.

WHY THE OBVIOUS DEFENSES DO NOT APPLY:
1. React does not block it. apps/frontend/node_modules/react-dom is 18.3.1, which only emits the "a future version of React will block javascript: URLs" warning and still renders the attribute.
2. `core/url_validation.py` is an outbound-SSRF module (WEBHOOK/LAN/OIDC policies for httpx clients). Every one of its ~20 call sites is an outbound fetch; it never touches `services.url`, which is a display-only link.
3. CSP does not intervene, though NOT for the reason the auditor gave. The auditor's claim that `'unsafe-inline'` leaves the door open is wrong: `'strict-dynamic'` is also present in `script-src`, and it causes `'unsafe-inline'` to be ignored, which does block `javascript:` URIs. The real gap is delivery: both `docker/nginx.mono.conf:323` and `docker/nginx.conf:163` define `location / { add_header Cache-Control "no-cache..."; try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html; }`. nginx inherits `add_header` from an outer level only when the current level declares none, so declaring Cache-Control there discards the server-level CSP (nginx.mono.conf:107) for `index.html` itself. The SPA document therefore loads with no CSP in the default Docker deployment, and the payload runs.

NO EXISTING COVERAGE: no test in apps/backend/tests, apps/frontend/src/__tests__, or tests/build asserts a scheme check on this field or a CSP header on the SPA document.

The codebase already recognises this bug class and guards the sibling case: `sanitizeImageSrc` in apps/frontend/src/utils/validation.js:9 ("Allow only safe URL protocols for image src attributes to prevent javascript: XSS"). It is applied only to `src`, never to any `href`.

CORRECTIONS TO THE AUDITOR: (a) the third sink, RemediationDrawer.jsx:90, is a FALSE POSITIVE - `guide.links` comes from `getRemediationGuide` in the static local module apps/frontend/src/data/remediationGuides.js and is not attacker-controlled; (b) the claim that no scheme helper exists is inaccurate - `sanitizeImageSrc` exists, just unused on hrefs.

SEVERITY: raised from the auditor's medium to high. It is stored, cross-user, and crosses a privilege boundary (editor -> whatever the viewer holds, including admin) with full same-origin script execution and no CSP to contain it. It stops short of critical only because it needs an authenticated editor plus one victim click. Note the click barrier is lower than it looks: ServiceDetail renders `{service.url}` as the visible link text, so the payload is legible there, but HardwareDetail.jsx:585 wraps the same href around an `<ExternalLink>` icon with `title="Open URL"`, so the payload is entirely invisible before the click.

title: `cb update` (docker mode) destroys the running container and recreates it without the operator's environment, then reports success on a crash loop
reasoning:
The auditor's headline framing is wrong and I reject it: docker-compose.yml sets `container_name: circuitbreaker` (line 22), while cb's docker-mode default is CB_CONTAINER="circuit-breaker" (cb:55). A compose deployment is never reached by this branch — `docker stop/rm circuit-breaker` are no-ops absorbed by `|| true` — so no hardened container is destroyed, and no compose hardening (read_only, cap_drop, no-new-privileges, tmpfs, limits, 8443, the helper socket) is "dropped on upgrade". The only install that actually owns a container named `circuit-breaker` is the documented single-container path (docs/installation/manual-docker.md:28), and that command sets none of those properties itself, so there is nothing to lose. `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` (cb:442) is a genuine but minor weakening relative to that documented command's default seccomp profile; compose never sets it, so it mirrors nothing.

What does survive scrutiny is the destructive/false-success half. Concrete path with default configuration: an operator follows manual-docker.md, runs the container named `circuit-breaker` with the four secrets passed as `-e` flags and `-p 127.0.0.1:8443:8443`, then installs cb by hand as docs/cb-cli.md:26 instructs. No installer writes install.conf — tests/build/test_cb_cli_contract.py::test_operator_supplied_paths_are_documented_as_such exists specifically to keep that true — so CB_MODE falls back to "docker" (cb:53) with only a _warn at cb:73. `cb update` then: pulls (cb:428), stops and removes the live container (cb:431-432), finds no `$CB_CONFIG_DIR/env` (cb:435 — also never created by anything, same test), and runs `docker run -d` with an empty env_args, `-p 8080:8080` and `-v circuit-breaker-data:/data`. docker/entrypoint-mono.sh:34-38 aborts FATAL on the absent CB_JWT_SECRET, and it does so *before* the `$DATA/.env` auto-sync at line 225, which only ever restores CB_VAULT_KEY anyway — so the volume cannot rescue it. `--restart unless-stopped` turns that into a restart loop. `docker run -d` exits 0 as soon as the container is created and started, so `|| _fail` at cb:445 cannot observe the exit-1 entrypoint, and cb prints "Updated and restarted." The old container is already gone, the listening port silently moved from 127.0.0.1:8443 to 0.0.0.0:8080, and CB_ALLOW_DIRECT_EGRESS is lost too. No guard exists anywhere in the call path: cmd_update's only preflight is _require_docker (cb:426), and the post-change `/api/v1/livez` poll that the restore path has at cb:632-641 was never added here. No test covers cmd_update's behaviour (tests/build/test_cb_cli_parity.py:27 only checks the command name is present).

Severity high, but for availability rather than the security reason given: the documented upgrade command reliably takes down the deployment it is meant to upgrade and reports success. Data is not lost (the named volume is reattached) and the operator can recover by re-running their original docker run, which is why this is not critical; the narrowing factor is that only hand-installed cb on the single-container path is affected.
fix:
Two changes in the docker branch of cmd_update, both matching conventions already in this file.

1. Refuse before destroying, not after — mirror the _require_docker/_require_binary "fail with a sentence" style. Move the env-file check above the stop/rm and make its absence fatal:

      local env_args=()
      if [[ -f "$CB_CONFIG_DIR/env" ]]; then
        env_args=(--env-file "$CB_CONFIG_DIR/env")
      else
        _fail "No environment file at $CB_CONFIG_DIR/env — the recreated container would start without CB_JWT_SECRET, CB_VAULT_KEY, CB_DB_PASSWORD and NATS_AUTH_TOKEN and exit FATAL. Write that file with the values this container was created with (see docs/cb-cli.md), or upgrade by re-running your original 'docker run'."
      fi

   then _info/stop/rm, then the docker run. Also drop `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` (cb:442): nothing in the shipped compose file or the documented run command asks for it, and it only weakens the default profile.

2. Verify the result instead of trusting `docker run -d`'s exit code, reusing the restore path's poll (cb:632-641) verbatim in shape, before printing success:

      if command -v curl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        _info "Waiting for the application to come back…"
        local tries=0
        until curl -fsS "http://127.0.0.1:${CB_PORT:-8080}/api/v1/livez" >/dev/null 2>&1; do
          tries=$((tries + 1))
          [[ $tries -gt 60 ]] && _fail "Updated, but the application did not become healthy. Check: cb logs"
          sleep 2
        done
      fi
      _ok "Updated and restarted."

Optional but cheap rollback insurance: replace `docker rm "$CB_CONTAINER"` with `docker rename "$CB_CONTAINER" "${CB_CONTAINER}-prev"`, and only remove -prev once the livez poll passes — so a failed upgrade can be undone with `docker rename`/`docker start`.

Since docs/cb-cli.md:92-94 currently claims the command "works without" ~/.circuit-breaker/env, that sentence has to change with the code, and the existing contract test's assertions about operator-supplied paths still hold (nothing new writes the file).

title: restore.sh replays the dump without ON_ERROR_STOP and reports success over a partially loaded database
reasoning:
Confirmed after trying to refute it on five separate grounds; all failed.

Line 199 is `zcat "$SNAP_DIR/db.sql.gz" | psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U "$CB_DB_OWNER" "$CB_DB_NAME"` with no ON_ERROR_STOP and no status check, immediately after lines 197-198 have dropped and recreated the database. psql's documented exit status is 3 for a script error ONLY when ON_ERROR_STOP is set; in default mode a failing statement goes to stderr, execution continues, and the process exits 0. zcat also exits 0, so `set -euo pipefail` (line 41) has nothing to trip on. Execution falls through to uploads, vault key, `systemctl start` and `echo "✓ Restore complete."`.

No guard exists elsewhere in the call path:
- cb:634-641 (the only post-restore check) polls /api/v1/livez, and main.py:2035-2042 documents that handler as "deliberately touches no dependency" — it returns 200 against an empty database.
- services/backup/verify.py validates archive members, the db.sql.gz sha256 and the vault-key hash. It inspects the archive, never the replay.
- restore.sh's own checks (steps 4-8) all run before anything is destroyed; nothing after line 199 inspects the result.

Not dead code, and the asymmetry is real rather than house style: cb:689 and cb:692 both run psql with `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` plus an explicit `|| _fail` for the container path. Only the native/binary path is missing it, and that path is reached two ways — `_restore_binary` (cb:752-805) for `binary` mode, and direct invocation, which docs/backup-restore.md:233-236 documents as the supported DR entry point for when `cb` or its install.conf is part of what was lost.

Reachable with shipped configuration. Migration 0050 (0050_timescaledb_hypertables.py:149-155) skips itself when timescaledb is unavailable, so hosts with and without hypertables are both supported states, and docker/run-postgres-if-embedded.sh:6 shows the extension additionally requires shared_preload_libraries=timescaledb. Replaying a hypertable-bearing pg_dump onto a rebuilt host missing that preload fails the CREATE EXTENSION and every dependent _timescaledb_internal chunk table, losing that data silently. The same silent-success shape follows from a PG major-version mismatch on the rebuilt host or a disk that fills during the COPY blocks.

No test covers it. test_restore_targets.py pins unit existence, layout defaults and vault-key destination; test_cb_cli_parity.py pins command surface. test_snapshot_roundtrip.py:68 does replay with ON_ERROR_STOP=1 — but in the test's own `_psql` helper, not through restore.sh, so the suite depends on the flag while the shipped script omits it.

Severity high rather than the reported critical: it needs an abnormal replay condition rather than firing on the happy path, and the `cb restore` route has already taken a safety snapshot (cb:614). But the documented direct-invocation DR route has no safety snapshot, the previous database is already gone, and the operator is told the restore succeeded.

One part of the report is wrong and I excluded it: the claim that an rsync failure at line 205 leaves the vault key unwritten "with no message". rsync failing exits non-zero under set -e, and cb:804 turns that into `_fail "Restore failed — see the output above."` It is visible and recoverable by re-running, and reordering would only mirror the hazard (key installed, uploads never synced). The finding stands on line 199 alone.
fix:
Add the flag and check the status explicitly, matching the `|| _fail` convention cb:689/692 already use for the container path. Replace line 199 with:

    if ! zcat "$SNAP_DIR/db.sql.gz" \
        | psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U "$CB_DB_OWNER" \
               -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 --single-transaction "$CB_DB_NAME"; then
        echo "ERROR: the dump did not replay cleanly — see the psql errors above." >&2
        echo "       The database was NOT restored. Common causes: this host's" >&2
        echo "       PostgreSQL lacks an extension the snapshot uses (timescaledb" >&2
        echo "       needs shared_preload_libraries), a role the dump grants to does" >&2
        echo "       not exist here, a major-version mismatch, or no disk space." >&2
        echo "       Fix the cause and re-run with the same snapshot." >&2
        exit 1
    fi

`-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1` is the load-bearing half. `--single-transaction` is worth pairing with it here: pg_dump's default plain output replays fine inside one transaction, and it turns a failure into an empty database rather than an arbitrary half-loaded one, which is what makes the error message above true. The `if !` form is required so errexit does not kill the script before the message prints; pipefail still catches a zcat failure.

title: run_upgrade's pre-upgrade pg_dump swallows every failure and unconditionally reports "Backup saved"
reasoning:
I tried to kill this one on three fronts (dead code, guard elsewhere, unshippable config) and it survived, though two of the auditor's three mechanisms do not.

CONFIRMED — the core defect is real and live:
- deploy/setup.sh:1588-1595 is exactly as reported: `pg_dump ... > "$backup_file" 2>/dev/null || true` followed by an unconditional `cb_ok "Backup saved: $backup_file"`.
- The path is NOT dead. `run_upgrade` is invoked from install.sh:765 (`if [[ "$UPGRADE_MODE" == "true" ]]; then run_upgrade; exit 0; fi`), and UPGRADE_MODE is set at setup.sh:389 whenever `/etc/circuitbreaker/.env` exists. This is the ordinary `cb update` path that docs/installation/upgrading.md tells every native/LXC operator to run.
- No guard exists anywhere downstream. I grepped the whole file: nothing re-tests `-s`/`-f "$backup_file"`, and `cb_ok` (install.sh) is a bare echo with no predicate. `|| true` neutralises `set -e` (line 2) before it can fire.
- No test covers it: no file under tests/ or apps/backend/tests/ references `pre-upgrade`, `backup_file`, or `Backup saved`.

The concrete trigger the auditor missed, and the one that makes this reachable on default config: line 1591 calls **bare `pg_dump`** with no `$PG_BIN_DIR` prefix and setup.sh never puts PG_BIN_DIR on PATH (no `PATH=` assignment exists in either script). Every other Postgres binary is invoked qualified — `"$PG_BIN_DIR/pg_ctl"` (438, 1384, 1502), `$PG_BIN_DIR/initdb` (461). On RHEL/Rocky/Alma/Fedora, stage2 installs PGDG `postgresql15-server postgresql15` and sets `PG_BIN_DIR="/usr/pgsql-15/bin"` (1499) — not on PATH. `/usr/bin/pg_dump`, if present at all, comes from the distro base `postgresql` package (PG13 on EL9). pg_dump *hard-aborts* against a newer server ("aborting because of server version mismatch"); psql only warns. That asymmetry is precisely why the existing psql probes at 519, 587 and 1153 all pass and never catch this. Absent base postgresql, it is plain `command not found`. Either way: zero-byte file, `|| true`, green "Backup saved". Disk exhaustion is a second real trigger — stage0 preflight only requires 3GB free, which a scan/topology database can exceed.

The artifact is also unrestorable even when the dump succeeds. verify.py:21 `_REQUIRED_MEMBERS = ("db.sql.gz", "vault.key", "manifest.json")` and verify.py:137 opens with `tarfile.open(path, "r:gz")` — a bare `pre-upgrade-*.sql` fails at the gzip-tarball open. So this line never produces something `cb restore` accepts, success or failure. That is the same class INC-15 closed (docs/1.0.0-incomplete-features.md:73). Contrast the Python builder: snapshot.py:84-89 runs `subprocess.run(["pg_dump", ...], check=True)` and raises BackupError — the app's own backup fails loudly while the installer's fails silently.

REFUTED — auditor mechanism (b), the missing `${CB_DATA_DIR}/backups` directory: essentially wrong for supported upgrades. setup.sh:137 has created it in stage1_bootstrap since commit b14536b6 (2026-03-18 06:09), which predates tag v0.2.4 (2026-03-18 20:39), and docs/release/1.0.0-compatibility-policy.md only supports direct 1.0 upgrades from >= 0.3.5. Every supported source install already has the directory. Only a v0.1.x/v0.2.2-lineage data dir would lack it. `mkdir -p` is still worth adding as cheap insurance, but it is not the failure mode.

OVERSTATED — auditor mechanism (a), pgbouncer transaction pooling: pool_mode = transaction is confirmed (deploy/config/pgbouncer.ini:10, rendered at setup.sh:566), but a single-threaded pg_dump wraps its entire data dump in one `BEGIN ... REPEATABLE READ, READ ONLY` transaction, which pgbouncer pins to a single server connection — the dump is consistent. Only pg_dump's pre-BEGIN session SETs are lost to `server_reset_query = DISCARD ALL`. This is contrary to PgBouncer's own guidance and worth correcting to 5432 (the port `CB_DB_URL` at setup.sh:35 and the snapshot builder both use), but it does not reliably yield an empty file and is not what makes this severe.

SEVERITY — high, not critical. This line destroys nothing on its own; it misreports. Harm requires a compound scenario: a bad upgrade plus an operator who trusted the console line over docs/installation/upgrading.md, which independently instructs "Always export and verify a backup before upgrading" and never advertises this artifact as the rollback path. But the scenario is entirely plausible — 1.0 forbids binary downgrade (ADR-0002, compatibility policy), making a pre-upgrade backup the only rollback — and the installer prints a specific filesystem path as proof of a backup that may not exist. False assurance on the last-resort recovery artifact, one step removed from data loss.
fix:
Minimal, convention-matching fix at deploy/setup.sh:1588-1596. Qualify the binary, keep stderr, drop the swallow, and gate the success message on a non-empty file:

  cb_step "Creating pre-upgrade backup"
  local backup_file="${CB_DATA_DIR}/backups/pre-upgrade-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).sql"
  if systemctl is-active circuitbreaker-pgbouncer &>/dev/null; then
    mkdir -p "${CB_DATA_DIR}/backups"
    # 5432 direct, not 6432: pgbouncer runs pool_mode=transaction, and the rest of
    # the product dumps against the direct port (CB_DB_URL). $PG_BIN_DIR because
    # PGDG installs pg_dump outside PATH on EL, and pg_dump — unlike psql — hard
    # aborts on client-older-than-server.
    if ! PGPASSWORD="$CB_DB_PASSWORD" "$PG_BIN_DIR/pg_dump" \
         -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5432 -U breaker circuitbreaker > "$backup_file" 2>>"$LOG_FILE" \
       || [[ ! -s "$backup_file" ]]; then
      rm -f "$backup_file"
      cb_fail "Pre-upgrade backup failed — refusing to upgrade without one" \
              "Check: tail -50 ${LOG_FILE}. Take a verified backup with 'cb backup', then re-run."
    fi
    cb_ok "Backup saved: $backup_file"
  else
    cb_warn "Database not running - skipping backup"
  fi

Note this changes behavior: a failed dump now aborts the upgrade instead of proceeding on a lie. That is the point — cb_fail already emits hints and diagnostics, and the operator can re-run. If aborting is considered too aggressive for the "pgbouncer down" case, that branch is already a cb_warn and is unaffected.

Follow-up worth filing separately (do not fold into this fix): the artifact is a bare .sql that `cb restore` structurally rejects (verify.py:137-153). Routing the pre-upgrade capture through the same snapshot builder `cb backup` uses (apps/backend/src/app/services/backup/snapshot.py, which emits db.sql.gz + vault.key + manifest.json) would make it actually restorable — but it needs a resolved vault key, so it is a design change, not a one-line edit.

title: install.sh never verifies the bundle checksum: it fetches a `.sha256` asset that no release publishes, and the missing `else` makes the skip silent
reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not; verification instead showed the defect is unconditional rather than conditional.

The code is as quoted (install.sh:545-561): `if [[ "$SKIP_CHECKSUM" == "true" ]] ... elif curl -fsSL -o "/tmp/${tarball_name}.sha256" "$checksum_url" 2>/dev/null; then ... fi`, with no `else`, falling through to `CB_BUNDLE_TARBALL="/tmp/${tarball_name}"` and then `tar -xzf` plus `cp -f ... /opt/circuitbreaker/bin/circuit-breaker; chmod 755; chown root:root` in stage0_install_bundle. Nothing between the fetch and the install re-checks integrity: the only later guards are `tar -xzf` succeeding and `[[ -f "${CB_BUNDLE_DIR}/circuit-breaker" ]]` existing, neither of which is an integrity check. `set -euo pipefail` does not apply — a false `elif` test is ordinary control flow.

The decisive point the auditor missed: `checksum_url="${tarball_url}.sha256"` names an asset that the project never produces. `.github/workflows/release.yml` generates a single combined `SHA256SUMS` (lines 242-246 and 396-400, `find . -maxdepth 1 -type f ! -name SHA256SUMS -exec sha256sum {} + > SHA256SUMS`), optionally signs it, and uploads `dist/release/*` via `gh release create`. A repo-wide grep for `\.sha256` outside of `sha256sum` returns only the four lines inside install.sh — no build script, packaging file, or workflow ever writes a per-asset `<tarball>.sha256`. A `browser_download_url` with an unknown asset name appended returns 404 from GitHub, so `curl -f` fails, the `elif` is false on every real release, and the branch is dead. The verification block has therefore never run in a default `curl -fsSL ... | sudo bash` install (README.md:55), and because there is no `else`, it prints nothing at all — the operator sees "Downloaded 47M" then "Extracting bundle", with no indication that the advertised check was skipped. `--skip-checksum` at least warns; the real path does not.

This also contradicts the project's own posture: SECURITY.md:54-63 and docs/installation/security-verification.md:13-17 tell manual downloaders to `gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.asc SHA256SUMS && sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS`, while the installer that runs as root does nothing equivalent.

No test covers it. tests/build/ has test_install_release_selection.py (release picking only) and test_build_script.py; grepping tests/build for checksum/sha256 yields only an unrelated nginx-route test and a PKGBUILD `sha256sums=('SKIP')` string. The other install path, `--local-bundle` (used by cb-proxmox-deploy.sh:441), is a separate branch and is out of scope.

On severity I part company with the auditor's reasoning while keeping the rating. The "attacker drops that one request" story is weak: both the API and the asset come over HTTPS from github.com, so a network attacker cannot selectively suppress the checksum without breaking TLS, and a checksum fetched over the same channel as the artifact adds little against MITM anyway. What makes it high is different and more concrete: a security control the project documents as present is inert on 100% of default installs, it fails open silently, and the thing it fails open on is a root-owned binary at /opt/circuitbreaker/bin/circuit-breaker installed by a piped-to-root script. It would not catch a corrupted or truncated CDN download, a swapped release asset, or a compromised-then-restored artifact — and no operator would ever learn the check did not happen.
fix:
Two changes, both inside the same block, in the style of the surrounding code.

1. Point at the asset that actually exists. Resolve `SHA256SUMS` from `release_json` next to where `tarball_url` is resolved (install.sh:534-538), rather than string-appending `.sha256`:

```bash
    local checksum_url
    checksum_url=$(echo "$release_json" | jq -r '.assets[] | select(.name=="SHA256SUMS") | .browser_download_url')
```

2. Verify against it and fail closed. Replace lines 545-559 with:

```bash
    # Verify checksum. SHA256SUMS covers every asset in the release, so
    # --ignore-missing restricts the check to the one file we downloaded.
    # The release workflow writes entries as `./<name>` (find . -maxdepth 1),
    # which resolves from /tmp where the tarball lives.
    if [[ "$SKIP_CHECKSUM" == "true" ]]; then
      cb_warn "Skipping SHA256 verification (--skip-checksum)"
    else
      cb_step "Verifying checksum"
      if [[ -z "$checksum_url" ]] || [[ "$checksum_url" == "null" ]]; then
        cb_fail "Release v${CB_VERSION} publishes no SHA256SUMS" \
          "Refusing to install an unverified bundle — use --skip-checksum only for a bundle you trust"
      fi
      curl -fsSL -o /tmp/cb-SHA256SUMS "$checksum_url" \
        || cb_fail "Could not fetch SHA256SUMS for the bundle" \
                   "Re-run, or use --skip-checksum only for a bundle you trust"
      if (cd /tmp && sha256sum --ignore-missing -c cb-SHA256SUMS >/dev/null 2>&1) \
         && grep -qF "./${tarball_name}" /tmp/cb-SHA256SUMS; then
        cb_ok "SHA256 checksum verified"
      else
        rm -f /tmp/cb-SHA256SUMS
        cb_fail "SHA256 mismatch — bundle may be corrupted or tampered" \
          "Use --skip-checksum to bypass (only for trusted local bundles)"
      fi
      rm -f /tmp/cb-SHA256SUMS
    fi
```

The `grep -qF` is load-bearing: `--ignore-missing` exits 0 when *no* listed file is present, so without it a SHA256SUMS that omits the tarball would pass. Note the `.sha256` cleanup on the mismatch path (current line 554) can go with it.

Worth adding a test alongside tests/build/test_install_release_selection.py asserting that the asset name install.sh fetches is one release.yml actually uploads — that class of drift is what made this dead rather than merely fragile. The auditor's GPG suggestion (packaging/circuit-breaker-release-key.asc, already uploaded by release.yml:429) is a reasonable follow-up, but SECURITY.md:56-62 says `.asc` files are produced only when a signing key is available, so it cannot be made mandatory in the installer without breaking unsigned releases — keep it a separate change.

title: install.sh --docker writes the vault key, JWT secret and DB password to a 0644 .env with no chmod
reasoning:
I went looking for the guard and there isn't one, anywhere in the call path.

Trace: `main()` (install.sh:738) dispatches `--docker` straight to `stage_docker_deploy` before any other stage — it explicitly skips `cb_require_native_root` and every preflight. Create the file inside a tightened umask so it is never 0644 even momentarily, and lock the containing directory — matching the acme_service.py "no chmod window" convention. In `stage_docker_deploy`:

At line 327, after the mkdir:
    mkdir -p "${install_dir}/docker"
    chmod 700 "${install_dir}"

At line 341, replace the bare cp:
    (umask 077; cp "${install_dir}/.env.example" "${install_dir}/.env")

The appends at 343-349 then inherit 0600. Nothing breaks: `docker compose` reads `.env` as the owning user (the `chown -R` at 356 hands it to `target_user`), and cb-helperd runs as root, so neither needs group or other read. title: One-time OAuth auth codes live in a per-process dict while the mono image runs 2 uvicorn workers
reasoning:

The cookie cannot substitute. When the exchange hits the other worker it raises HTTPException(400) at line 63; the frontend only `console.error`s (line 281-283), the code has already been stripped from the URL by `history.replaceState('/oobe')`, so it is not retryable, and the wizard silently flips to `localAccountRequired` — the user who just completed a Google/GitHub/OIDC round trip is bounced to "Account details are invalid" and forced into a local password account. title: One-time OAuth auth codes live in a per-process dict while the shipped image runs `uvicorn --workers 2`, so `/auth/exchange` fails ~50% of the time
reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could only knock down half of it.

Mechanism confirmed:
- `apps/backend/src/app/api/auth_oauth.py:33` `_pending_auth_codes` is a plain module-level dict, written by `_issue_auth_code` (:37) from `_issue_jwt_and_redirect` (:437) and `_bootstrap_redirect_or_none` (:473), and read by `exchange_auth_code` (:61) on a *separate* HTTP request from the SPA (`apps/frontend/src/api/auth.js:85`).
- `docker/supervisord.mono.conf:110` really is `uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --workers 2`, and `docker-compose.yml:21` builds `Dockerfile.mono`, so this is the default shipped deployment, not an exotic config.
- `docker/nginx.mono.conf` has no `upstream` block and no `keepalive` pool — it does a plain `proxy_pass $backend` per request, so each request is a fresh connection that the kernel hands to whichever of the two workers accepts it. Nothing pins the exchange to the worker that handled the callback. The two workers are forked at boot, long before any code is minted, so no copy-on-write sharing helps.
- No guard exists anywhere on the path: `exchange_auth_code` has only `@limiter.limit` and a `Query(...)` constraint. There is zero test coverage — `grep -rn "auth/exchange\|_pending_auth_codes" apps/backend/tests` returns nothing.
- The project's own `core/security.py:93-105` comment ("The app ships behind `uvicorn --workers 2`, so the per-process cache alone meant a logout handled by worker A left worker B honouring the same token") documents exactly this hazard for the session cache and routes it through Redis; the auth-code store was never migrated. Redis is present in the same image (`supervisord.mono.conf` `[program:redis]`) and `agent_enrollment.consume_pairing_code` (`apps/backend/src/app/services/agent_enrollment.py:81-98`) already implements the exact GETDEL pattern needed.

Where the auditor overstated it: the *ordinary login* flow is almost entirely masked, and the report is wrong about `LoginPage.jsx:131`. `_issue_jwt_and_redirect` also sets the httpOnly `cb_session` cookie on the same 302 (`core/auth_cookie.py:set_auth_cookie_on_response`), and `AuthContext.jsx:73-85` calls `authApi.me()` on mount; `App.jsx:348` blocks rendering until `authReady`. With a valid cookie `isAuthenticated` is true, so `App.jsx:155` (`path="/"` → `Navigate to="/map"`) renders and LoginPage never mounts — the `?cb_auth_code=` is simply dropped unexchanged. LoginPage's exchange effect only runs when the cookie session check has already failed, so "about half of all attempts show 'OAuth login failed'" is not right.

Where it is genuinely real and unmasked: the OOBE OAuth bootstrap. When `needs_bootstrap` is true, `App.jsx:396` routes *every* path to `OOBEWizardPage`, and `OOBEWizardPage.jsx:262-281` must get the raw JWT *value* into JS — the cookie cannot substitute, because `submitBootstrap` (:604-609) sends `oauth_token: oauthBootstrapToken` in the `POST /bootstrap/initialize-oauth` body. A failed exchange is swallowed into `console.error` (:279-281), the wizard still advances to step 4 and skips the account step, and at finish `localAccountRequired = !oauthBootstrapToken` (:567) is true with empty account fields, so the user is bounced back to step 3 with "Account details are invalid." That is a ~50% failure rate on first-run OAuth setup in the default Docker image, with the only diagnostic in the browser console. This is a first-class shipped flow: OOBE step 3 writes the provider config via `PATCH /settings/oauth` and then redirects to `/api/v1/auth/oauth/<provider>` (:508-562).

Severity medium rather than high: it hits only the OAuth-bootstrap path (local-account bootstrap and post-setup OAuth login are unaffected/masked), it is recoverable by retrying, and it is a reliability defect, not a security one — no code is leaked or replayable across workers, the pop is still single-use within a worker.
fix:
Move the code→token map to Redis with the same GETDEL pattern `agent_enrollment` uses, keeping the in-process dict as the Redis-unavailable fallback (matching the "Redis unreachable ⇒ degraded, not broken" convention in `core/security.py`). All three call sites (`auth_oauth.py:679/682`, `788/791`, `923/926`) are inside `async def` callbacks, so the helpers can become async without touching any sync caller:

```python
_AUTH_CODE_KEY_PREFIX = "cb:oauth:authcode:"
_AUTH_CODE_TTL = 60.0


async def _issue_auth_code(token: str) -> str:
    """Store *token* under a one-time random code valid for _AUTH_CODE_TTL seconds.

    Written to Redis so either `uvicorn --workers 2` process can redeem it — the
    browser's /auth/exchange call is a separate connection and need not land on
    the worker that handled the provider callback.
    """
    from app.core.redis import get_redis

    code = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    r = await get_redis()
    if r is not None:
        await r.setex(f"{_AUTH_CODE_KEY_PREFIX}{code}", int(_AUTH_CODE_TTL), token)
        return code
    now = time.monotonic()
    for k in [k for k, (_, exp) in _pending_auth_codes.items() if now > exp]:
        del _pending_auth_codes[k]
    _pending_auth_codes[code] = (token, now + _AUTH_CODE_TTL)
    _logger.warning("Redis unavailable — auth code is redeemable only on this worker")
    return code


@router.get("/exchange")
@limiter.limit(lambda: get_limit("auth"))
async def exchange_auth_code(request: Request, response: Response, code: str = Query(...)) -> dict:
    from app.core.redis import get_redis

    r = await get_redis()
    if r is not None:
        # GETDEL is atomic server-side, so the code cannot be redeemed twice.
        val = await r.getdel(f"{_AUTH_CODE_KEY_PREFIX}{code}")
        if val is not None:
            return {"token": val.decode() if isinstance(val, bytes) else str(val)}
    entry = _pending_auth_codes.pop(code, None)
    if entry is None or time.monotonic() > entry[1]:
        raise HTTPException(400, "Invalid or expired auth code")
    return {"token": entry[0]}
```

Then `await` the two mint sites and make their enclosing helpers async: `_issue_jwt_and_redirect` (:425) and `_bootstrap_redirect_or_none` (:444) become `async def`, with `code = await _issue_auth_code(token)` at :437 and :473, and the six call sites at :679/682, :788/791, :923/926 gain `await`. Update the module comment at :30-31 ("stored in process memory only") to say Redis-backed with an in-process fallback. Worth adding the missing regression test: mint a code, clear `_pending_auth_codes` to simulate the other worker, and assert `/auth/exchange` still returns the token when Redis is up.

(3) The suggested fix is incomplete: forwarded_client_identity alone does not inspect the socket peer, so on a direct connection to uvicorn (or a deployment whose proxy is outside trusted_proxy_cidrs) it returns the attacker's own forged hop; it must be gated by request_from_trusted_proxy the way core/rate_limit.py:89-96 does. reasoning:
Confirmed for ws_telemetry.py; the ws_monitors.py half of the auditor's claim is refuted.

_MAX_SUBSCRIPTIONS (line 53) is referenced exactly twice in the module: its definition and the per-message slice entity_ids[:_MAX_SUBSCRIPTIONS] at line 263. Nothing ever inspects len(subscribed_channels), so line 273's set.update() is a pure accumulator across frames.

Each frame can add 200 fresh channel strings, retained for the connection's lifetime.

Reachable on default configuration:
- Auth (lines 196-218) requires only a valid JWT for an active, unlocked, non-demo-expired user. Unlike ws_monitors.py, this module never imports or calls has_scope/effective_scopes, so a read-only account qualifies.
- The CIDR gate defaults to "[]" (line 223) and core/network_acl.is_ip_in_cidrs documents "[]" as "allow all", so it is open out of the box.
- middleware/rate_limit_middleware.py is a BaseHTTPMiddleware and additionally short-circuits when current_tenant_id is None (the normal single-tenant v1 path); nothing rate-limits WebSocket frames anywhere in the tree.
- _check_limits caps sockets (100 global / 10 per IP), not per-socket state.

Impact does not depend on Redis: when get_redis() returns None the listener parks on stop_event (lines 96-99) and the set still grows in the API process. With Redis up it is worse, because lines 274-284 tear down and re-issue pubsub.subscribe(*channels) over the entire accumulated set on every frame, making the work O(n) per message with n client-controlled, plus per-channel subscription state inside Redis.

Refutation of the ws_monitors.py:422 part of the report: that call site feeds from _authorized_monitor_channels() (line 287), which for each id calls monitor_service.get_monitor() and only adds a channel when the row exists and passes reader_can_access_monitor. No existing coverage: grep for subscription_limit / MAX_SUBSCRIPTIONS across apps/backend/tests returns nothing, and test_rel07_listener_recovery.py only exercises listener fault recovery.

Severity medium rather than high: availability-only, no data path, and it requires an authenticated session, so it is not pre-auth. It is not lower than medium because the privilege required is the least the system issues and the module's own design (connection cap, per-IP cap, CIDR gate) shows per-socket resource limits were intended here.

Separate observation, not this finding: ws_telemetry.py performs no per-entity authorization on telemetry:{id} at all, while ws_monitors.py does. That is a confidentiality issue worth its own report.

Cap the accumulated set, not the frame. Replace line 273 with:

    subscribed_channels.update(new_channels)
    if len(subscribed_channels) > _MAX_SUBSCRIPTIONS:
        await websocket.send_text(json.dumps({"error": "subscription_limit_exceeded"}))
        await websocket.close(code=1008)

Place it immediately after the update and before the listener teardown/re-creation at lines 274-284, so an overflowing frame does not pay the O(n) resubscribe. Do not apply this to ws_monitors.py:422 — its channel set is already bounded by _authorized_monitor_channels()'s DB existence and access checks.

title: verify_audit_chain/repair_audit_chain fully materialise the logs table, including the untruncated body columns the hash never covers
reasoning:
Traced and confirmed, with one of the auditor's sub-claims corrected.

Reachable path: admin authenticates -> GET /api/v1/audit-log/verify-chain (apps/backend/src/app/api/admin_audit.py:22, guarded only by require_role("admin"), no query params, no pagination) -> verify_audit_chain(db) -> `list(session.execute(select(Log).order_by(Log.id.asc())).scalars().all())`. The rows are genuinely fat, and worse, fat with data the function does not need. canonical_log_payload (line 22) covers only created_at_utc, action, actor_id, role_at_time, entity_type, entity_id, diff, ip_address, previous_hash. The impact lands harder than "a worker restarts". The default deployment is the mono container with `memory: 2G` (docker-compose.yml:57-63) shared with PostgreSQL, nginx, NATS and Redis, so an OOM kill during the scan takes the database down with the API. The endpoint is a plain `def`, so it also holds an anyio executor thread for the entire scan, and being a GET it is trivially re-triggered.

The obvious refutation does not hold. "The chain walk is inherently sequential over every row, so it must load them" is false: the loop carries only `previous_hash` between iterations, so yield_per streaming is a drop-in with no algorithmic change. And repair does not need the prefix at all -- verify_audit_chain has already proven every row before first_failure_id recomputes to its stored log_hash, so previous_hash entering the repair segment is exactly the stored log_hash of the preceding row.

I did check the usual escape hatches and none apply: the code path is live (admin_audit.py is the sole non-test caller and is routed), the endpoint takes no attacker-shaped input that a validator could reject, no dependency or middleware bounds the result set, and no test covers volume (tests/test_logs.py:167-215 and tests/services/test_audit_spool.py exercise correctness with a handful of rows).

Correcting the auditor on one point: the claim that repair's `.with_for_update()` blocks concurrent appends is not the real mechanism. log_service._do_write takes the audit-chain advisory lock at line 208 before its `select(Log).order_by(Log.id.desc()).limit(1).with_for_update()` at line 209, and repair_audit_chain takes that same advisory lock at line 199 -- appends are already serialised there by design. The row locks widen lock scope but introduce no new blocking class. Repair is nonetheless worse than verify for a reason the auditor missed: it walks the table three times inside one transaction (verify at 189, the FOR UPDATE select at 194, verify again at 250), and the rows it mutates become dirty and are held by strong reference in the session until flush() at 221, so its peak is the whole table and cannot be collected mid-walk the way verify's clean instances can.

Severity medium rather than high: it is availability-only, requires admin credentials, and needs a table that has grown large through sustained real use. Not low, because the default 2G mono container makes the failure a full-stack outage and the trigger is a repeatable GET.
fix:
Two changes, both minimal and local to audit_chain.py.

1. Stream verify_audit_chain and stop loading the columns the hash never covers. Add `from sqlalchemy.orm import Session, load_only` and replace lines 135-136:

    stmt = (
        select(Log)
        .options(
            load_only(
                Log.created_at_utc,
                Log.action,
                Log.actor_id,
                Log.role_at_time,
                Log.entity_type,
                Log.entity_id,
                Log.diff,
                Log.ip_address,
                Log.previous_hash,
                Log.log_hash,
            )
        )
        .order_by(Log.id.asc())
        .execution_options(stream_results=True, yield_per=1000)

Then iterate the result directly instead of materialising it -- drop `logs = list(...)`, walk `for checked_count, log in enumerate(session.execute(stmt).scalars(), start=1)`, keep a `checked_count = 0` initialised before the loop, and replace the two post-loop uses of `len(logs)` (lines 169-170) with that counter. The empty-table early return at 138-144 becomes `if checked_count == 0:` after the loop. The instances are clean here, so the Session's weak identity map lets each batch be collected as the walk advances, and peak memory becomes the yield_per window rather than the table.

2. Stop repair_audit_chain from loading and locking the prefix. verify_audit_chain has already established that every row before first_failure_id recomputes to its stored log_hash, so seed the walk from that row instead of replaying the chain from id 1. Replace line 194 with:

    seed = session.execute(
        select(Log.log_hash).where(Log.id < first_failure_id).order_by(Log.id.desc()).limit(1)
    ).scalar_one_or_none()
    logs = list(
        session.execute(
            select(Log).where(Log.id >= first_failure_id).order_by(Log.id.asc()).with_for_update()
        ).scalars()
    )

and initialise `previous_hash: str | None = seed` at line 195. Every row selected is now one the repair segment actually rewrites, so `in_repair_segment` and the `log.id == first_failure_id` test at 202-204 collapse away -- the loop body becomes the unconditional rewrite. This bounds both the materialised set and the FOR UPDATE lock to the damaged suffix, and leaves the advisory lock at 199 as the sole (intended) serialisation point against concurrent appends.

Add a regression test alongside tests/test_logs.py:199 that seeds a few thousand rows with large old_value/new_value payloads and asserts verify_audit_chain still reports valid, so the streaming path stays covered.

title: Outbound SSRF validation resolves DNS but connects by hostname — rebinding reopens the window
reasoning:
Confirmed. `validate_outbound_url` resolves the host and checks every answer, stores them in `ValidatedURL.addresses` (line 192) — and nothing ever reads that field. A repo-wide grep finds only the dataclass declaration, the assignment, and one test assertion at apps/backend/tests/unit/test_url_validation.py:78. `safe_async_request` then hands `validated.url` (the hostname form) to `client.request()` at line 221, so httpx performs a second, independent `getaddrinfo` at connect time.
